chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.h: Bank M11 — Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distribut
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of Exercise 2 of the examples PDF (TechNova Solutions), for a supplier that sells to firms, with one short numeric part on the price elasticity of demand as in Exercise 1 (d). The company is invented. Concepts: Topic 5, Slides 17 (elasticity), 24-25 (range of products and life-cycle), 27-28 (price) and 34-37 (distribution); topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-3; Examples PDF, Exercises 1 and 2.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: Altamira Cabin Systems, founded in 2009 in Getafe (Madrid), designs and manufactures galley and lavatory equipment for commercial aircraft. In 2026 its range has two product lines: galley inserts (the ovens G1 and G2 and the coffee maker C1) and lavatory modules (the models L1 and L2). Every product is certified for, and installed in, the cabins of commercial aircraft. For 2027 the board has approved three changes: it will launch a new oven, the G3, for long-haul aircraft; it will stop making the lavatory module L1, whose sales have fallen every year since 2022 because the new aircraft no longer use it; and it will open a third line of food trolleys for high-speed trains (the models R1 and R2), to be sold to railway operators.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
The G2 oven costs Altamira 8,000 € per unit, and its price is set by adding 35% to that cost. The trolleys R1 and R2 will be priced 5% below the equivalent trolleys of the market leader. The price of the coffee maker C1 was fixed after asking twenty airlines how much they would be willing to pay for it. The commercial director's objective is to reach 15% of the European market of galley inserts by 2029. Altamira sells 500 G2 ovens a year; very few ovens are certified for the aircraft that use it, and the sales department estimates the price elasticity of demand of the G2 at 0.5 in absolute value. The board is considering a 6% rise in the price of the G2.

Ovens and lavatory modules for new aircraft are sold directly to the two aircraft makers that install them on their assembly lines, by Altamira's own team of key-account engineers, who visit each customer every month. Spare units and the equipment that airlines buy when they refurbish their cabins are sold through one authorised distributor per continent: an independent firm that buys the products from Altamira, stores them and resells them to airlines and maintenance companies. Each distributor holds the sole right to sell Altamira products in its continent.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
a) Describe the range of products of Altamira in 2026 and after the three changes of 2027 (extension or width, depth of each line, length and consistency). Which product strategy of the course is each change, and which stage of the product life-cycle explains the withdrawal of the L1? (0.75 points)

b) Which approach to pricing does Altamira use for the G2, for the trolleys and for the coffee maker? Calculate the price and the mark-up of the G2, and say which fact of the second paragraph is a pricing objective and not a pricing approach. (0.5 points)

c) If Altamira raises the price of the G2 by 6%, calculate the new expected sales volume and the sales revenue of the G2 before and after the rise. Is the demand elastic or inelastic, and why? What would the revenue be if the elasticity were 1.6? (0.75 points)

d) Describe the two distribution channels of Altamira: type and length, B2B or B2C, and the distribution intensity of the network of distributors. Is the team of key-account engineers a distribution channel? (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
| Item | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Unit cost of the G2 | 8,000 € |
| Rule of the G2 price | cost plus 35% |
| Present sales of the G2 | $Q = 500$ ovens a year |
| Price elasticity of demand of the G2 | $\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.5$ |
| Price change of part (c) | $+6\%$ |
| Alternative elasticity of part (c) | $\lvert E_d \rvert = 1.6$ |

Model of the course: the elasticity of the demand is the percentage variation in the demand divided by the percentage variation in the factor [Topic 5, Slide 17]; for the price, the coefficient is negative and its absolute value is used [topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2]. As in Exercise 1 (d) of the examples PDF, the percentage change in the quantity is the elasticity times the percentage change in the price, with the opposite sign [Examples PDF, Exercise 1 (d)]. Sales revenue is the price times the quantity [topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3].

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: Count the lines, the products of each line and the products in total, before and after. For consistency, ask whether every product still has the same final use.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
- 2026: extension 2 lines; depth 3 (galley inserts) and 2 (lavatory modules); length 5; consistency high (all for aircraft cabins).
- 2027: extension 3; depth 4, 1 and 2; length 7; consistency lower (the train trolleys have another final use).
- G3: extend a product line (more depth). Train trolleys: add a product line (more range). L1: the opposite of extending a line, depth of the lavatory line from 2 to 1.
- L1: decline stage (obsolescence), sales falling since 2022.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
#### The range in 2026 and in 2027

A range of products is an offer of product lines and individual products, described by its extension (number of lines), depth (products per line), length (total number of individual products) and consistency (with the final use of the product) [Topic 5, Slide 24]. The examples PDF calls the extension the width (breadth) of the range [Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 3].

| Characteristic | 2026 | 2027 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Extension (width) | 2 (galley inserts, lavatory modules) | 3 (plus train trolleys) |
| Depth | galley 3 (G1, G2, C1); lavatory 2 (L1, L2) | galley 4 (G1, G2, G3, C1); lavatory 1 (L2); trolleys 2 (R1, R2) |
| Length | $3 + 2 = 5$ | $4 + 1 + 2 = 7$ |
| Consistency | high: every product is "installed in the cabins of commercial aircraft" | lower: the trolleys are used in high-speed trains, another final use |

#### Strategy behind each change

Slide 24 lists three product strategies: add more product lines (more range), extend the product lines (more depth) and incorporate product variations (more length) [Topic 5, Slide 24].

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
- New oven G3 in the galley line: extend a product line; the depth of the galley line rises from 3 to 4.
- Line of trolleys R1 and R2: add a product line; the extension rises from 2 to 3. It is also the change that lowers the consistency, because the new products do not share the final use of the others.
- Withdrawal of the L1: the reverse of extending a line; the depth of the lavatory line falls from 2 to 1 and the length falls by one.

The length goes from 5 to $5 + 1 + 2 - 1 = 7$: the G3 and the two trolleys add three products and the L1 removes one.

#### Why the L1 is withdrawn

"Sales have fallen every year since 2022 because the new aircraft no longer use it": the L1 is in the decline stage of its life-cycle, the stage of obsolescence [Topic 5, Slide 25]. It is not maturity, the longest part of the curve, where sales stay high.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: Slide 28 gives three approaches: competition, demand and cost (cost-plus pricing or break-even analysis). Ask what each price is built from: a cost, the price of a rival or what the customer would pay.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
- G2: cost approach, cost-plus pricing; price $8{,}000 \times 1.35 = 10{,}800$ €; mark-up 2,800 € per oven.
- Trolleys: competition approach (5% below the leader).
- Coffee maker C1: demand approach (what twenty airlines would pay).
- Pricing objective: 15% of the European market of galley inserts, a market-share objective.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
#### The approach of each price

Slide 28 distinguishes the competition approach, the demand approach and the cost approach, which uses cost-plus pricing or break-even analysis [Topic 5, Slide 28].

| Fact of the text | Approach of the course |
| :--- | :--- |
| G2: "set by adding 35% to that cost" | Cost approach, cost-plus pricing |
| Trolleys: "5% below the equivalent trolleys of the market leader" | Competition approach |
| C1: "after asking twenty airlines how much they would be willing to pay" | Demand approach |

#### Price and mark-up of the G2

The mark-up is the difference between the cost of a good and its selling price [Topic 5, Slide 28].

$$p_{G2} = 8{,}000 \times (1 + 0.35) = 10{,}800\ \text{€}$$

$$\text{Mark-up} = p_{G2} - \text{cost} = 10{,}800 - 8{,}000 = 2{,}800\ \text{€ per oven}$$

#### Objective, not approach

"Reach 15% of the European market of galley inserts by 2029" says what the prices should achieve, not how they are computed: it is a pricing objective, achieving a certain market share, one of the three objectives of Slide 27 with maximizing profit and maximizing sales [Topic 5, Slide 27].

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: Write the percentage change of the quantity from the elasticity, then multiply the new price by the new quantity. Compare the revenue before and after, and remember what an elasticity below 1 means.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
- New price: $10{,}800 \times 1.06 = 11{,}448$ €.
- Change in quantity: $-0.5 \times 6\% = -3\%$; new volume 485 ovens.
- Revenue: 5,400,000 € before; 5,552,280 € after; change +152,280 €.
- Inelastic demand ($\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.5 < 1$): few certified substitutes, so the revenue rises.
- With $\lvert E_d \rvert = 1.6$: $-9.6\%$, 452 ovens, revenue 5,174,496 €, a fall of 225,504 €.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
#### New price and new quantity

The price rises by 6% from the price of part (b):

$$p_1 = 10{,}800 \times (1 + 0.06) = 11{,}448\ \text{€}$$

From the elasticity, the percentage change in the quantity is the elasticity times the percentage change in the price, with the opposite sign [Examples PDF, Exercise 1 (d)]:

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{Q} = -\lvert E_d \rvert\,\frac{\Delta p}{p} = -0.5 \times 6\% = -3\%$$

$$Q_1 = 500 \times (1 - 0.03) = 485\ \text{ovens}$$

#### Revenue before and after

$$I_0 = p_0\,Q_0 = 10{,}800 \times 500 = 5{,}400{,}000\ \text{€}$$

$$I_1 = p_1\,Q_1 = 11{,}448 \times 485 = 5{,}552{,}280\ \text{€}$$

$$\Delta I = 5{,}552{,}280 - 5{,}400{,}000 = 152{,}280\ \text{€}$$

#### Elastic or inelastic

$\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.5 < 1$, so the demand of the G2 is inelastic: a 1% change in the price moves the quantity by less than 1% [Topic 5, Slide 17]. With an inelastic demand a price rise sells nearly the same quantity at a higher price, and the revenue rises [topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3], as found above. The reason is in the text: "very few ovens are certified for the aircraft that use it", and the elasticity depends mainly on the availability of substitute goods [topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2].

#### With an elasticity of 1.6

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{Q} = -1.6 \times 6\% = -9.6\%, \qquad Q_1' = 500 \times (1 - 0.096) = 452\ \text{ovens}$$

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
$$I_1' = 11{,}448 \times 452 = 5{,}174{,}496\ \text{€}, \qquad \Delta I' = 5{,}174{,}496 - 5{,}400{,}000 = -225{,}504\ \text{€}$$

With $\lvert E_d \rvert = 1.6 > 1$ the demand would be elastic: the quantity falls by more than the price rises and the revenue falls [topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3]. The same 6% rise helps or hurts the revenue depending only on the elasticity.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: For each channel, ask whether an independent firm takes the title of the product between Altamira and the final buyer, who that buyer is, and how many distributors there are in each area.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
- New aircraft: direct channel, zero levels (Altamira to aircraft maker), B2B.
- Spares and refurbishment: indirect channel, one level (Altamira, distributor, airline or maintenance company), the distributor acts as a wholesaler, B2B.
- Intensity of the distributors: exclusive, one distributor per continent with the sole right to sell.
- The key-account engineers are not a channel: they are Altamira's own sales force (personal selling, a promotion tool) inside the direct channel.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x:
#### Channel for new aircraft

"Sold directly to the two aircraft makers": the producer sells directly to the final buyers, a direct channel [Topic 5, Slide 35], with no intermediary, the zero-level channel of the TechNova case [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (c)]. The buyers are firms, so it is business-to-business (B2B).

#### Channel for spares and refurbishment

"An independent firm that buys the products from Altamira, stores them and resells them to airlines and maintenance companies": an independent intermediary takes the title, so the channel is indirect [Topic 5, Slide 35]. It sells to organizational buyers and not to final consumers, which is what the course calls a wholesaler [Topic 5, Slide 35]; the storage is one of the functions of the intermediaries [Topic 5, Slide 36]. Extension: the level of a channel is the number of intermediaries between the producer and the final buyer; this one has one level (Altamira, distributor, airline). The buyers are again firms: B2B.

"One authorised distributor per continent ... the sole right to sell Altamira products in its continent" is exclusive distribution [Topic 5, Slide 37]. Extension (definition not given on the slide): exclusive distribution grants a single outlet per area, against a limited number of chosen outlets (selective) or as many as possible (intensive).

#### The key-account engineers

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: A distribution channel is a series of interdependent firms that transfer the title of the product from the producer to the final buyer [Topic 5, Slide 34]. The engineers are Altamira's own employees, so they add no level to the channel: they are the firm's sales force, and their monthly visits are personal selling, a tool of the promotion mix [Topic 5, Slide 33]. The channel of the new aircraft stays direct and zero-level.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
chunks.x: Altamira's buyers are few, large and technical firms, so its marketing rests on the range, the price and a short channel rather than on mass communication. The inelastic demand of a certified oven makes a price rise profitable in revenue, while the train trolleys widen the range at the cost of its consistency and are priced against the leader of a market in which Altamira is a newcomer.

chunks.t: Altamira Cabin Systems: range of products, pricing approaches, a price rise and exclusive distributors
Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.h: Bank M12 — Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercise 3 of the examples PDF, centred on the organizing function: factors that determine the structure, parts of the formal structure, configurations, the informal structure and the managerial roles of Mintzberg. The firm is fictitious. Content: Topic 6, Slides 9, 11-16, 20 and 22. The deck only names the Mintzberg roles and the word "departmentalization (types)"; the one-line meaning of each role and the names of the departmentalization criteria other than functional and matrix are given here as an **extension**.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
Kestrel Drones was founded four years ago by Lucía Ferrer, an aeronautical engineer, with eight colleagues. Until last year the firm had 25 people: Lucía decided everything, from the price of each contract to who flew which test, and every engineer, pilot and technician reported to her directly. Nobody had a fixed job: the same engineer designed a wing in the morning and repaired a customer's drone in the afternoon, and there was no written procedure, because "we just ask Lucía".

After a large investment round the firm has grown to 180 employees and now sells two very different product lines: light crop-survey drones for farm cooperatives in Spain and Portugal, and heavy inspection drones for electricity grid operators across Europe, which must pass a certification by the aviation authority. Each line has its own customers, its own sales cycle and its own engineering team. Lucía no longer has time to approve every decision: offers wait weeks for her signature, two customers received drones with different software versions, and the certification audit found that test flights were not recorded in a standard way.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
The founders who joined in the first year still meet Lucía every Friday afternoon and settle many questions there, outside any meeting on the calendar; newcomers say that "the real decisions are taken at the Friday coffee". In a normal week Lucía also opens the firm's stand at a drone trade fair, negotiates the terms of the investment round, reassigns two engineers when a prototype crashes during a test, and reads the reports on a competitor's new drone before telling the engineering teams what she has learnt.

Tasks:

a) Using the factors that determine the organizational structure, describe how the structure of Kestrel Drones was four years ago and how it must change now. (0.5 points)

b) State which parts of the formal structure the firm had at the start and which parts must appear with the growth, linking each new part to a problem of the statement. (0.5 points)

c) Name the basic organizational configuration of the firm at the start, propose the configuration it should move to and the type of departmentalization, and justify the choice. (0.5 points)

d) Identify the informal structure in the case, explain how it differs from the formal one and what the real structure is, and say how management should treat it. (0.5 points)

e) Classify the activities of Lucía described in the last paragraph into the managerial roles of Mintzberg, naming the group of each role. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: The course lists five factors: specialization (horizontal and vertical), standardization, formalization, centralization and the structural configuration (departmentalization, number of layers, span of control, size of the administrative component).

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
- Specialization: low before ("nobody had a fixed job"), higher now (one engineering team per line).
- Standardization and formalization: almost none before ("no written procedure"), needed now (software versions, recorded test flights for certification).
- Centralization: total before ("Lucía decided everything"), decentralization needed now (offers waiting weeks).
- Structural configuration: one layer and a very wide span of control before; more layers, a smaller span and an administrative component now.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
#### Specialization

Specialization is horizontal (the number of tasks a person does) and vertical (the autonomy to organize one's own job) (Topic 6, Slide 13). Before, horizontal specialization was low: "the same engineer designed a wing in the morning and repaired a customer's drone in the afternoon". Now each product line has "its own engineering team", so horizontal specialization rises: people concentrate on fewer tasks of one line.

#### Standardization and formalization

Standardization is how far work follows set rules and procedures, and formalization how far those rules are written down (Topic 6, Slide 13). Before there was "no written procedure", so both were very low. Now the two customers with "different software versions" and the test flights "not recorded in a standard way" show that standardized procedures are needed, and the certification by the aviation authority requires them to be written: both factors must increase.

#### Centralization

Before, decision-making was fully centralized: "Lucía decided everything" (Topic 6, Slide 13). Now "offers wait weeks for her signature", which shows that one person can no longer take every decision for 180 employees: decisions on offers, tests and production must be decentralized to the heads of each line.

#### Structural configuration

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: Before there was a single layer between Lucía and everybody, with a span of control of about 25 people and no administrative component. Now the firm needs departments, at least one more hierarchical layer (heads of line), a smaller span of control for each manager and an administrative component that handles certification, quality and finance (Topic 6, Slide 13).

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: Slide 14 gives five common parts: strategic apex, middle line, operating core, technostructure and support staff. Slide 15 says which parts a simple structure has.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
- At the start: only the strategic apex (Lucía) and the operating core (engineers, pilots, technicians).
- Middle line: heads of each product line, so that offers do not wait for Lucía.
- Technostructure: analysts who write the standard procedures (software versions, test-flight records for certification).
- Support staff: units outside the operating workflow (legal, finance, human resources).

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
#### The parts at the start

A simple structure has only a strategic apex and an operating core (Topic 6, Slide 15). At Kestrel Drones the **strategic apex** (top management) was Lucía, and the **operating core** (the employees who do the basic work) were the engineers, pilots and technicians who "reported to her directly" (Topic 6, Slide 14).

#### The parts that must appear

- **Middle line** (middle management): a head for the crop-survey line and a head for the grid-inspection line, who approve offers and assign people inside their line; this removes the bottleneck of "offers wait weeks for her signature".
- **Technostructure** (analysts who design systems and processes): a quality and certification office that designs the procedure for releasing a software version and the standard record of every test flight, the two failures found in the statement.
- **Support staff** (outside the operating workflow): units such as legal, finance and human resources, which handle the investment round, the contracts and the hiring of the 155 newcomers without doing the engineering work itself.

All five parts are listed in Topic 6, Slide 14.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: Compare the facts with the five configurations of Slides 15-22. Two product lines with their own customers, cycles and teams point to one of them; check what the course says about the key part and the environment of each.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
- At the start: simple structure (entrepreneurial start-up), strategic apex as key part, direct supervision, only apex and operating core.
- Proposal: division organization, with one division per product line (departmentalization by product and market); middle line as key part; top management coordinates performance and outputs; diversified businesses, dynamic environment.
- Alternatives (machine bureaucracy, adhocracy) discussed and rejected or accepted with reasons.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
#### The configuration at the start

With 25 people, Lucía as the key part deciding by **direct supervision** and only strategic apex and operating core, Kestrel Drones was a **simple structure (entrepreneurial start-up)**, the configuration of start-ups and very small businesses (Topic 6, Slide 15).

#### The proposed configuration

The firm now sells "two very different product lines", each with "its own customers, its own sales cycle and its own engineering team", in a changing market just funded by an investment round. This matches the **division organization**: autonomous divisions, the middle line as the key part, top management coordinating the performance and outputs of the divisions, used by diversified businesses in more dynamic environments (Topic 6, Slide 20). The departmentalization proposed is therefore **by product and market**: a crop-survey division and a grid-inspection division (**extension**: grouping by product, by customer or by geographic area are the usual criteria besides functional and matrix; the deck only says "departmentalization (types)", Topic 6, Slide 13). Inside each division the work can be grouped by function, because each division is itself a bureaucracy (Topic 6, Slide 20); the quality and certification office can serve both.

#### Why not the other configurations

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: A **machine bureaucracy** (functional departmentalization, centralized decisions, many layers, for mature firms in a stable and simple environment, Topic 6, Slide 16) would keep one engineering department for two very different lines and keep decisions at the top, the present problem. An **adhocracy** (matrix departmentalization, low standardization and formalization, Topic 6, Slide 22) suits specific projects, but certification demands written, standard procedures; it can still be used as a complementary structure for the design of a new drone. A reasoned answer that proposes a functional structure for a single-line firm is also valid, but here the two lines with separate customers make the division organization the better fit.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
- Fact: the Friday afternoon meetings of the founders with Lucía, "outside any meeting on the calendar"; "the real decisions are taken at the Friday coffee".
- Formal structure: defined by management (the new chart of divisions). Informal structure: contacts, communications and ways of doing things that employees develop.
- Real structure: formal plus informal.
- Management should not ignore it: use it for communication, but keep the decisions of the new heads of division in their formal channel.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
#### The informal structure in the case

The **informal structure** is the informal contacts, communications and ways of doing things that the employees develop (Topic 6, Slide 12). At Kestrel Drones it is the Friday afternoon meeting of the first-year founders with Lucía, held "outside any meeting on the calendar", where "many questions" are settled, so that newcomers feel that "the real decisions are taken at the Friday coffee".

#### Formal versus informal, and the real structure

The **formal structure** is the one defined by management (Topic 6, Slide 12): the divisions, heads and offices of parts (b) and (c), drawn in the organization chart, its graphic representation (Topic 6, Slide 11). The **real structure** is the combination of both (Topic 6, Slide 12): at Kestrel Drones, the new chart plus the influence of the founders' group.

#### How management should treat it

The informal structure cannot be abolished by drawing a new chart. Lucía should keep it as a fast channel of communication, but take the decisions of each line inside the division, with its head present; otherwise the new middle line would be bypassed and decisions would stay as centralized as before.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: Slide 9 gives three groups: interpersonal roles (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational roles (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson) and decisional roles (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
- Opening the stand at the trade fair: figurehead (interpersonal).
- Negotiating the investment round: negotiator (decisional).
- Reassigning two engineers after the crash: disturbance handler and resource allocator (decisional).
- Reading the competitor's reports: monitor; telling the teams: disseminator (informational).
- The Friday meetings with the founders: leader or liaison (interpersonal), accepted when reasoned.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x:
#### Meaning of the roles

The deck lists the ten roles in three groups (Topic 6, Slide 9). The one-line meaning used below follows Mintzberg and is an **extension**: the figurehead performs symbolic duties for the firm; the leader motivates and directs the people; the liaison keeps contacts outside the manager's own unit; the monitor gathers information; the disseminator passes it inside the firm; the spokesperson transmits it outside; the entrepreneur starts change and new projects; the disturbance handler deals with unexpected problems; the resource allocator decides who gets which resources; the negotiator bargains with other parties for the firm.

#### Classification of the activities

| Activity in the statement | Role | Group |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "opens the firm's stand at a drone trade fair" | figurehead (spokesperson if she presents the drones to visitors) | interpersonal (informational) |
| "negotiates the terms of the investment round" | negotiator | decisional |
| "reassigns two engineers when a prototype crashes" | disturbance handler; resource allocator | decisional |
| "reads the reports on a competitor's new drone" | monitor | informational |
| "telling the engineering teams what she has learnt" | disseminator | informational |

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: The Friday meetings with the founders also show her as **leader** (interpersonal role). Launching the second product line was a role of **entrepreneur** (decisional). With the division organization of part (c), part of the disturbance handler and resource allocator roles inside each line passes to the heads of division, while the figurehead, negotiator and entrepreneur roles stay at the strategic apex.

chunks.t: Kestrel Drones outgrows its simple structure
chunks.x: The case is the passage, as a firm grows, from the simple structure to a configuration with a middle line, a technostructure and a support staff (Topic 6, Slides 13-15). The symptoms of the statement (offers waiting for the founder, two software versions, unrecorded test flights) are each the lack of one factor or one part of the structure, and the informal Friday meeting shows that the real structure is more than the new organization chart (Slide 12). The roles of Mintzberg (Slide 9) describe what the founder does today and which of those roles she must hand over to the new middle line.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.h: Bank M13 — Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercise 3 of the examples PDF, centred on the four functions, the types and levels of decisions, human resources management and controlling. The firm is fictitious. Content: Topic 6, Slides 3-5, 7-8, 10-11, 14-16, 18 and 22-25. KPIs are not defined in the Topic 6 deck: they are taken from Examples PDF, Exercise 3, and treated as an **extension**. The trap of part (e): unlike a flexible working method, a programme of written, standard procedures is easiest in the machine bureaucracy.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
Orbis Aerostructures is a plant of 2,400 employees that machines and assembles fuselage panels and wing ribs for two aircraft manufacturers. Its operators do short, repetitive tasks on each workstation, every task follows a written work instruction, decisions are taken at the top and pass down through seven hierarchical levels, and a methods office designs the instructions. Last year one panel in every twenty-five was rejected at the customer's incoming inspection, mostly for drilling and sealing defects, and one manufacturer has warned that it will move part of its orders if the figure does not halve within a year.

The board of directors has approved a **quality-control and training programme** for the whole plant. Other plants of the same group solved a similar problem with programmes of this kind, but Orbis must adapt them to its own parts and machines. The programme has these actions:

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
1. Set the target "rejections below one panel in fifty within twelve months" and the calendar of the programme.
2. Create a quality cell in each production line, with a quality inspector who reports to the head of quality.
3. Hire twelve new quality inspectors, since nobody in the plant holds the inspection certificate.
4. Train the 900 operators of drilling and sealing in the new inspection checklists.
5. Explain to the operators in meetings on every shift why the programme matters for the plant's orders.
6. Pay a quarterly bonus to the lines that meet the target, and assess each operator's work every six months.
7. Measure every week the rejections at the customer and the defects found inside the plant, and correct the lines that fall behind.
8. Buy two new automatic drilling machines.

In each shift, the shift supervisor decides every morning which operators attend that day's training session, following the rota set by the training office.

Tasks:

a) Classify the actions 1 to 8 into the four managerial functions, and say which action is not a managerial function. (0.5 points)

b) Classify by type of decision and by management level: the board's decision to launch the programme, and the supervisor's daily choice of who attends the session. Say which managerial skill weighs most in each case. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
c) Using the activities of human resources management, explain how Orbis should recruit, select, train, appraise and compensate its people in the programme, and say which actions belong to directing and which to staffing. (0.5 points)

d) Define three KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) to control the programme and classify the control of action 7 by when it takes place and by its frequency. (0.5 points)

e) State in which basic organizational configuration this programme is easiest to introduce and in which it is hardest, justifying each answer with the features of the configuration. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: The four functions are planning, organizing, leading and controlling (Slides 3-4). In the course, leading is human resources management: directing and staffing (Slide 23). Ask of each action whether it sets goals, arranges people, manages people or compares results with the plan.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
- Planning: action 1.
- Organizing: action 2.
- Leading (human resources management): actions 3, 4, 5 and 6.
- Controlling: action 7.
- Action 8 (buying machines) is an investment and an operation of the production function, not a managerial function.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
#### Planning: action 1

Planning is setting goals and deciding on the strategy to achieve them, and a goal is a specific achievement to be attained at a future date (Topic 6, Slide 10). Action 1 sets exactly such a goal, "below one panel in fifty within twelve months", and its calendar.

#### Organizing: action 2

Organizing arranges the human resources so that their activities contribute to the firm's goals, by dividing and coordinating the work (Topic 6, Slide 11). Action 2 creates a new unit, the quality cell, and fixes who reports to whom: it changes the organization chart.

#### Leading: actions 3, 4, 5 and 6

Leading is human resources management (Topic 6, Slides 2 and 23). Hiring inspectors (3), training operators (4), explaining the programme on every shift (5), and the bonus and the six-monthly assessment (6) all manage people; part (c) sorts them into directing and staffing.

#### Controlling: action 7

Controlling ensures that activities provide the planned results: standards, measurement of actual performance, deviations and corrective action (Topic 6, Slide 24). Action 7 measures rejections and defects every week against the target of action 1 and corrects the lines that fall behind: planning and controlling are inseparable (Topic 6, Slide 24).

#### What does not belong: action 8

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: Buying two drilling machines is an investment decision and part of the production process, not one of the four managerial functions. Like "communication is not a product attribute" in Exercise 2 of the examples PDF, it is the item that does not belong to the list of the course.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: Slide 5 places a decision between routine and innovative by its problem and its alternatives; Slide 7 gives the levels (top: strategic, general; lower: tactical, functional); Slide 8 the skill that weighs most at each level.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
- Board decision: adaptable decision (known problem of rejections, alternatives known from the group's other plants but to be adapted); top management, strategic and general; conceptual skill.
- Supervisor's choice: routine (planned) decision (known, well-defined problem, known alternatives, a rota); low management (first-line supervisor), operational; technical skill.
- Interpersonal skill weighs at every level.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
#### The board's decision

The problem, rejections of drilled and sealed panels, is known and measured, and "other plants of the same group solved a similar problem", so the alternatives are partly known; but Orbis "must adapt them to its own parts and machines". It is neither a routine decision (known problem, known alternatives) nor an innovative one (unusual problem, ambiguous and not planned alternatives): it is an **adaptable decision**, between the two (Topic 6, Slide 5). It affects the whole plant and its relation with the customers, so it is a **strategic, general** decision of **top management** (Topic 6, Slide 7), where the skill that weighs most is the **conceptual skill**, seeing the firm as a whole (Topic 6, Slide 8).

#### The supervisor's daily choice

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: Choosing which operators attend today's session is a problem that is known and well defined, with known alternatives fixed by the rota of the training office: a **routine (planned) decision** (Topic 6, Slide 5). It is taken by a first-line supervisor, **low management**, and concerns one shift on one day, an operational decision of the lower levels of the pyramid, which the course calls tactical and functional by scope (Topic 6, Slide 7). The skill that weighs most there is the **technical skill**, knowing how the workstations operate and who can leave them (Topic 6, Slide 8). The interpersonal skill weighs at every level, for the board and for the supervisor alike.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: Slide 23: human resources management is the process of recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and compensating employees; it involves directing (motivation, leadership and communication) and staffing (recruiting, selecting and training; performance appraisal, compensation and incentive programmes). Recruitment and selection are two different activities.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
- Recruiting: attract candidates holding the inspection certificate (action 3).
- Selecting: choose the twelve inspectors among them.
- Training: action 4, the 900 operators.
- Appraising: the six-monthly assessment (action 6).
- Compensating: the quarterly bonus as an incentive programme (action 6).
- Directing: action 5 (communication, motivation); staffing: actions 3, 4 and 6.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
#### The five activities

Human resources management is the process of recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and compensating employees, and its problem is to align individual interests with the objectives of the company (Topic 6, Slide 23). In the programme:

- **Recruiting:** attract candidates for the twelve inspector posts, since "nobody in the plant holds the inspection certificate"; for example, a job offer to people who hold it.
- **Selecting:** choose the twelve best among the candidates attracted, for example with a test of measurement and inspection of a panel. Recruitment builds the pool, selection chooses from it; confusing them is the usual error.
- **Training:** action 4, the 900 operators of drilling and sealing learn the new checklists.
- **Appraising:** the six-monthly assessment of each operator's work (action 6), a performance appraisal system.
- **Compensating:** the quarterly bonus to the lines that meet the target (action 6), an incentive programme that ties the operators' interest to the objective of action 1.

#### Directing and staffing

**Directing** is motivation, leadership and communication: action 5, the shift meetings that explain why the programme matters. **Staffing** is recruiting, selecting and training, plus appraisal, compensation and incentives: actions 3, 4 and 6 (Topic 6, Slide 23).

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a measurable indicator of whether an objective is being achieved (Examples PDF, Exercise 3; **extension**). Slide 25 classifies control by who, by what area, by when (reactive, proactive, interactive) and by frequency (constant, periodic, occasional).

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
- Three measurable KPIs linked to the target: rejection rate at the customer, internal defect rate per line, share of operators trained (or inspections passed first time).
- Action 7 is periodic (weekly) control.
- By when: it reacts to defects already produced (reactive), with the in-plant measurement allowing correction before the panels ship (interactive part); reasoned answers accepted.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
#### Three KPIs

A KPI is a quantified measure of performance against an objective (Examples PDF, Exercise 3; **extension**). It is the measure of actual performance that controlling compares with the standard (Topic 6, Slide 24).

1. **Customer rejection rate:** panels rejected at the customer's incoming inspection divided by panels delivered, per month; the standard is the target of action 1, below one in fifty (2%), from one in twenty-five (4%) today.
2. **Internal defect rate per line:** drilling and sealing defects found by the quality cell per hundred panels, per week and per line, which shows the lines that fall behind.
3. **Training coverage:** operators of drilling and sealing who have completed the checklist training divided by the 900 planned, per month.

Other valid KPIs: share of panels passing inspection first time, hours of rework per panel, number of lines receiving the bonus.

#### Type of control of action 7

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: By **frequency**, action 7 is **periodic** control: it takes place every week, not constantly or only occasionally (Topic 6, Slide 25). By **when**, measuring rejections at the customer is **reactive**: it acts after the defect has happened. The weekly in-plant count of defects lets the quality cells correct a line before more panels are shipped, which brings it close to **interactive** control. **Proactive** control would act before the defects appear, as the training of action 4 does. By area, it controls each production line, a unit of the plant (Topic 6, Slide 25).

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: This programme is not a flexible way of working: it is a set of written, standard inspection procedures designed by analysts and imposed on the whole plant. Ask which configuration coordinates by standardization and has a technostructure, and which one has neither.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
- Easiest: machine bureaucracy (standardization and very formal procedures in the operating core, routine specialized tasks, centralized decisions, elaborate administrative structure); Orbis already is one, and its methods office is the technostructure that writes the checklists.
- Hardest: adhocracy (low standardization and formalization, technostructure disappears, decentralization); also accepted: professional bureaucracy, where qualified professionals standardize their skills and decide on their own work, or the simple structure, which has no technostructure.
- The trap: the opposite of the answer for an agile or flexible methodology (Examples PDF, Exercise 3).

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x:
#### Easiest: machine bureaucracy

The **machine bureaucracy** has many rules and very formal procedures in the operating core, highly specialized routine tasks, functional departmentalization, centralized decision-making and an elaborate administrative structure with many layers (Topic 6, Slide 16). Orbis already shows these features: "short, repetitive tasks", "a written work instruction" for every task, decisions "taken at the top" through "seven hierarchical levels", and a methods office that "designs the instructions", which is its **technostructure**, the part that designs systems and processes (Topic 6, Slide 14). A programme of new written checklists, decided by the board and applied to every line, uses the configuration's own way of coordinating: standardization. It is therefore easiest there.

#### Hardest: adhocracy

The **adhocracy** has low standardization and formalization, decentralization as the key to flexibility, and in it the technostructure disappears (Topic 6, Slide 22). Nobody would write the checklists and nobody would impose them across teams that organize their own work, so a plant-wide programme of standard procedures is hardest there.

#### Alternative answers

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: The **professional bureaucracy** is also a reasoned answer for "hardest": highly qualified professionals with standardization of their skills and knowledge, and decentralized decisions (Topic 6, Slide 18), resist a checklist written by analysts for their work. The **simple structure** has only a strategic apex and an operating core, so it has no technostructure to design the programme (Topic 6, Slide 15). The trap is to answer as in Exercise 3 of the examples PDF, where an agile methodology was hardest in the machine bureaucracy and easiest in the adhocracy: what is easy or hard depends on what is introduced, flexibility or standardization.

chunks.t: Orbis Aerostructures launches a quality and training programme
chunks.x: The case covers the four functions as one cycle (Slides 3-4): the target of planning (action 1) is the standard of controlling (action 7), and organizing and human resources management (Slides 11 and 23) carry it out. The two decisions of part (b) show that the type of decision and the level of the manager change together (Slides 5, 7 and 8). The configuration of part (e) is the opposite of the one that suits a flexible methodology, because a quality programme of written procedures relies on the standardization that defines the machine bureaucracy (Slide 16).

chunks.t: Voltaris hybrid-electric regional aircraft
chunks.h: Bank M14 — Voltaris hybrid-electric regional aircraft
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercises 2 and 3 of the examples PDF, which has no Topic 7 exercise. Voltaris Aero, Brenner Turbines, Litheon Cells, Kestrel Power, Fjordair, Mercator Regional and Alcudia Air are fictitious companies. Concepts and definitions: Topic 7, Slides 10-16.

chunks.t: Voltaris hybrid-electric regional aircraft
chunks.x: Voltaris Aero, founded by engineers who had designed electric motors for sports cars, is developing the VX-19, a 19-seat regional aircraft for routes of up to 400 km. Instead of two turboprop engines, its wing carries eight electric motors with small propellers, fed by a battery pack and by a turbo-generator bought from Kestrel Power, a maker of ground power units; wing, propellers, batteries and flight-control software had to be designed together, because the air blown by the eight propellers over the wing changes its lift. The cells of the pack come from Litheon Cells, a maker of cells for electric cars. Litheon has just launched a cell with a silicon anode that stores 15% more energy per kilogram, with the same format, connectors and cooling as its previous cell, so it fits the VX-19 pack unchanged. On its existing car-cell line, Litheon has also added an automatic X-ray inspection station before packing, which has cut defective cells from 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000.

chunks.t: Voltaris hybrid-electric regional aircraft
chunks.x:
Brenner Turbines has built turboprop engines, with their reduction gearboxes and variable-pitch propellers, for forty years; it supplies the engines of most of today's 19-seat aircraft. Its last three engine generations cost 180, 260 and 390 million euros to develop and cut fuel burn per seat-kilometre by 6%, 3% and 1.2% respectively. Litheon's cells, on the other hand, gained little for years (from 160 to 190 Wh/kg between 2010 and 2016) and then quickly (300 Wh/kg in 2024). Today the VX-19 still flies only 400 km, against 1,500 km for a turboprop aircraft of the same size.

The target market has 200 regional airlines. In the first year 4 airlines ordered the VX-19, among them Fjordair, an island-hopping airline whose managers follow every new propulsion technology closely and whose routes are all shorter than 250 km. After three years 30 airlines in total have ordered it. Mercator Regional, a large operator, says it will order "once ten airlines have flown it for two years without trouble"; Alcudia Air, a small family-owned airline with old aircraft, will "only buy when nobody sells turboprops any more".

chunks.t: Voltaris hybrid-electric regional aircraft
chunks.x:

| Product / process innovation | embodied in the outputs / a change in the way the organization conducts its business, often to improve effectiveness or efficiency (fewer defects, more output) | Topic 7, Slide 11 |
| Radical / incremental | very new and different from prior solutions / a relatively minor change to existing practices | Topic 7, Slide 12 |
| Competence-enhancing / destroying | builds on / renders obsolete existing knowledge and skills; depends on whose perspective is taken | Topic 7, Slide 12 |
| Architectural / component | changes the overall design of a system or the way its components interact / changes components without significantly affecting the overall configuration | Topic 7, Slide 13 |

#### Brenner Turbines: competence-destroying

Brenner's forty years of knowledge are in "turboprop engines, with their reduction gearboxes and variable-pitch propellers". In the VX-19 the propellers are driven by electric motors and the only turbine, the turbo-generator, is "bought from Kestrel Power". The innovation renders Brenner's existing skills obsolete for this aircraft [Topic 7, Slide 12].

#### Litheon Cells and Voltaris Aero: competence-enhancing

Litheon makes "cells for electric cars", and the VX-19 needs a battery pack: the innovation builds on its existing knowledge base and opens a new market to it. Voltaris's founders "had designed electric motors for sports cars", the same knowledge the eight motors use [Topic 7, Slide 12].

#### Why the answers differ

The same innovation enhances the competences of two firms and destroys those of a third: whether an innovation is competence-enhancing or competence-destroying depends on whose perspective is taken, so the firm must always be named [Topic 7, Slide 12].

#### Brenner's turboprop

The improvement obtained per 100 million euros of development effort falls from $6/1.8 = 3.33\%$ to $3/2.6 = 1.15\%$ and then to $1.2/3.9 = 0.31\%$. Each generation costs more and yields less: on the S-curve of performance against effort, the turboprop is in the flat upper part, approaching the limit of the technology [Topic 7, Slide 14].

#### Litheon's cells

The cells "gained little for years (from 160 to 190 Wh/kg between 2010 and 2016) and then quickly (300 Wh/kg in 2024)": the slow first part of the S-curve is over and the technology is in its steep middle part [Topic 7, Slide 14]. The path of the specific energy through time is the technology trajectory of the cells, measured as its rate of performance improvement [Topic 7, Slide 10].

#### A discontinuous technology

Hybrid-electric propulsion fulfils the same market need, carrying 19 passengers on regional routes, by building on an entirely new knowledge base (electric motors, batteries, distributed propulsion), so it is a discontinuous technology [Topic 7, Slide 15]. As the second technology of Slide 15, it starts below the first one ("400 km, against 1,500 km") but improves fast, while the turboprop is near its limit; if the trend continues, the second curve may overtake the first, which is the threat Brenner faces given part (b).

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.h: Bank M15 — Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercises 2 and 3 of the examples PDF, which has no Topic 7 exercise. Aurelia Smallsat, Terravista, Nordsat and the other organizations are fictitious. Concepts and definitions: Topic 7, Slides 3-9, 13 and 17-19.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
Until a decade ago every small satellite was designed from scratch around its payload. Aurelia Smallsat sells instead the AB-12, a standard bus: structure, power, attitude control, radio and on-board computer are always the same, and the customer's payload is fixed to a standard mechanical and electrical interface. Aurelia grew out of a student satellite programme of its region's polytechnic university, which the company still sponsors and from which it recruits most of its graduates. It started in a science park and incubator run by the regional government, and a national space agency grant paid for the in-orbit demonstration of the first bus. The standard payload interface was not invented by Aurelia: Terravista, an Earth-observation customer, had designed it for its own cameras because it was tired of re-wiring each one to a different satellite, and gave it to Aurelia.

The firm is located in a valley where thirty space firms (payload makers, ground-station operators, test laboratories) buy from and sell to each other and run joint research projects. Two engineers who left Nordsat, a neighbouring rival, joined Aurelia and brought with them Nordsat's know-how on testing radios under vacuum.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
During the last year Aurelia made three changes to the AB-12: (1) a new star tracker, more precise, which fits in the same slot with the same connector and data format; (2) deployable solar panels in place of body-mounted ones, a modest gain in power that nevertheless forced Aurelia to move the antennas and rewrite the attitude-control software, because the open panels change how the satellite turns; (3) a cheaper on-board computer that replaces the old one board for board.

Forty AB-12 buses now fly for twenty-two operators. Each flight has raised the reliability of the bus, and Aurelia reinvests the income in it. More and more payload makers sell cameras and radios "ready for the AB-12 interface", ground-station operators offer software for it, and two launch providers sell dispensers sized for it. A Nordsat manager answers that "a design can only become the industry standard if an authority imposes it"; Aurelia's chief executive adds that, once the AB-12 dominates, the firms of the sector "will keep developing completely new buses as much as now".

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x: Go through the players of Slides 3 and 8 and the ranked sources of Slide 6, without forgetting individuals and users; then the two features of networks of Slide 9.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
- Users as a source: Terravista designed the interface for its own needs (customers' technology).
- University: student programme, sponsored university research, recruited students.
- Government-funded research: science park and incubator, agency grant.
- Technology cluster: the valley of thirty firms (buyers, suppliers, joint research).
- Technological spillover: Nordsat's know-how carried by two engineers.
- The linkages among them as the main source.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
#### Sources of innovation

- **Users:** Terravista "had designed it for its own cameras because it was tired of re-wiring each one", a user who designs a solution for its own needs, one of the individual sources of Slide 3; for Aurelia it is customers' technology, a source of development work in the ranking of Slide 6 [Topic 7, Slides 3 and 6].
- **Universities:** Aurelia "grew out of a student satellite programme" of a polytechnic university, "still sponsors" it and "recruits most of its graduates": sponsored university research and recruited students are ranked third and fourth among firms' sources of research work [Topic 7, Slides 6 and 8].
- **Government-funded research:** a "science park and incubator run by the regional government" and "a national space agency grant", two of the channels through which governments invest in research [Topic 7, Slide 8].
- **Firms:** Aurelia itself, with the incentive to develop a differentiating product (the standard bus) [Topic 7, Slide 3].

#### Collaborative networks

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
- **Technology cluster:** "thirty space firms ... buy from and sell to each other and run joint research projects" in one valley: a regional cluster connected to a common technology, with buyer and supplier relationships and research collaboration, helped by proximity [Topic 7, Slide 9].
- **Technological spillover:** the engineers from Nordsat "brought with them Nordsat's know-how on testing radios under vacuum": knowledge spreads across organizational boundaries, a positive externality of Nordsat's R&D [Topic 7, Slide 9].
- No single player made the AB-12: the linkages among user, university, government and cluster are, as the course says, the most important source of innovation [Topic 7, Slide 4].

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
- Standard bus with a standard payload interface: architectural (new way bus and payload interact).
- Star tracker: component. On-board computer: component.
- Deployable panels: architectural, although the gain is modest (antennas moved, attitude software rewritten).

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
#### The standard bus

Compared with satellites "designed from scratch around its payload", the AB-12 separates bus and payload through a standard interface: the overall design of the satellite and the way its parts interact change, an **architectural** innovation [Topic 7, Slide 13].

#### The three changes

- **Star tracker: component.** It "fits in the same slot with the same connector and data format": one component changes without affecting the overall configuration [Topic 7, Slide 13].
- **Deployable solar panels: architectural.** The gain in power is "modest", but the change "forced Aurelia to move the antennas and rewrite the attitude-control software, because the open panels change how the satellite turns": the way the components interact changes, which is what defines an architectural innovation [Topic 7, Slide 13]. The trap is to call it component because it is small: the pair is about the configuration of the system, not about the size of the improvement.
- **On-board computer: component.** It "replaces the old one board for board" [Topic 7, Slide 13].

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x: Slides 18 and 19: one force inside the firm, one on the side of the users, and their result. Slide 17 says what kind of standard a dominant design is.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
- Learning effects: reliability rises with each flight, income reinvested; absorptive capacity (graduates, Nordsat know-how).
- Network externalities: installed base (40 buses, 22 operators); complementary goods (payloads, ground software, dispensers).
- Result: winner-take-all tendency; usually 50% or more of the market.
- The manager confuses a de facto standard with an imposed one; regulation is not a course factor (extension).

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
#### Learning effects

"Each flight has raised the reliability of the bus, and Aurelia reinvests the income in it": the more the technology is used, the more it is developed and the more effective it becomes, and adoption generates revenue that is reinvested in refining it [Topic 7, Slide 18]. Aurelia's absorptive capacity, its ability to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge (the university's graduates, the testing know-how from Nordsat), speeds the process [Topic 7, Slide 18].

#### Network externalities

The value of the AB-12 to an operator grows with the number of other operators that use it [Topic 7, Slide 19]:

- **installed base:** "forty AB-12 buses now fly for twenty-two operators";
- **complementary goods:** cameras and radios "ready for the AB-12 interface", ground-station software and launch dispensers "sized for it", goods and services that enhance the value of the bus. The more of them there are, the more attractive the bus is to the next operator, which in turn attracts more complements.

#### Dominant design and the manager's statement

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x: These two forces push the market towards winner-take-all: the AB-12 could reach usually 50% or more of the small-satellite market and become its dominant design, while alternative platforms survive in niche markets [Topic 7, Slides 17 and 19]. The Nordsat manager is wrong for the course: a dominant design is a **de facto standard**, a standard of the industry even if it is not officially enforced, selected by learning effects and network externalities [Topic 7, Slide 17]. An imposed standard is a different case: a standard set by regulation, that is, by a rule of a public authority that firms must obey, is an **extension** beyond the course, which gives no role to regulation in the selection of a dominant design.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
- After the selection, producers and customers focus on efficiency in manufacturing, delivering, marketing or deploying the dominant design, rather than developing alternatives.
- The chief executive is wrong: completely new buses will be developed less, not "as much as now".
- Alternatives survive only in niche markets.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x:
#### What follows the selection

Once the dominant design is selected, producers and customers focus their efforts on improving their efficiency in manufacturing, delivering, marketing or deploying it, rather than continuing to develop alternative designs [Topic 7, Slide 17]. In this case, effort would go into building AB-12 buses faster and cheaper, integrating payloads on them, and component improvements such as the star tracker and the on-board computer of part (b).

#### The chief executive's claim

The claim that the firms "will keep developing completely new buses as much as now" contradicts the course: the development of alternative architectures falls after the selection, and the platforms that remain outside the dominant design survive in niche markets [Topic 7, Slides 17 and 19], for example satellites whose payload is too large or too unusual for a standard bus.

chunks.t: Aurelia standard small-satellite bus
chunks.x: The AB-12 itself is an architectural innovation born from a network (a user, a university, government programmes and a cluster), and its chance of dominating rests on the two forces of Part III of Topic 7, not on an official decision. A small change can be architectural, and after a dominant design emerges the effort of the sector moves from developing alternative designs to making and deploying the dominant one more efficiently.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. New sales of the cooperative

$$75 \times 0{,}90 = 67{,}5 \text{ u./month}, \qquad 67{,}5 \times 25 = 1.687{,}5 \text{ m.u./month}, \qquad 12 \times 1.687{,}5 = 20.250 \text{ m.u.}$$

$$\Delta\text{Revenue} = 20.250 - 20.700 = -450 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Revenue} = 87.750 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 2. Raw material (hypothesis 4)

In the base case 4.500 tons were consumed for 3.600 units: $4.500 / 3.600 = 1{,}25$ t/unit $= 2{,}50$ m.u./unit. Selling $12 \times 7{,}5 = 90$ units fewer:

$$\Delta\text{Consumption} = -90 \times 2{,}50 = -225 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{final stock} = 1.800 + 225 = 2.025 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 3. New results

$$\text{Profit before taxes} = 24.000 - 450 + 225 = 23.775, \qquad \text{Tax} = 0{,}25 \times 23.775 = 5.943{,}75$$

$$\text{Net profit} = 23.775 - 5.943{,}75 = 17.831{,}25, \qquad \text{Remaining} = 17.431{,}25$$

$$\text{Reserves} = 0{,}60 \times 17.431{,}25 = 10.458{,}75, \qquad \text{Dividends} = 0{,}40 \times 17.431{,}25 = 6.972{,}50$$

#### Step 4. New cash

The cooperative now pays at 60 days: January to October collected, $10 \times 1.687{,}5 = 16.875$ instead of 20.700 (−3.825). The dividend paid falls by 67,50; the tax is not paid in 2018.

$$\text{Cash} = 14.060 - 3.825 + 67{,}50 = 10.302{,}50 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 5. Changes in the statements

**Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the discount** (18.000 against 17.831,25): removing the discount gains $2$ m.u. on each of the 810 units the cooperative still buys ($810 \times 2 = 1.620$ m.u.), but the 90 units it stops buying carried a margin over raw material of $23 - 2{,}50 = 20{,}50$ m.u. each ($90 \times 20{,}50 = 1.845$ m.u.); the net effect before taxes is $1.620 - 1.845 = -225$ m.u. The **cash is also higher with the discount** (14.060 against 10.302,50): the cooperative pays in the same month, while under the general condition November and December stay as receivables. Keeping the discount wins on both counts.

- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit and tons × m.u./ton give m.u.; m.u./year × months/12 gives m.u.; ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why ROA and ROE are so high:** the company's annual sales (88.200 m.u.) are ten times its 2017 assets; the ratios are measured on the year-end balance, which already includes most of the year's profit.
- **Accrual vs cash:** net profit 18.000 m.u., but cash grew by only 13.120 m.u. because 11.250 m.u. of sales are uncollected, although many expenses (tax, software, raw material, renting) are still unpaid.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
The external auditor of **TALLERES AERONÁUTICOS DEL HENARES S.A. (TAHSA)**, a company of Alcalá de Henares dedicated to the machining of titanium brackets and fittings for the aircraft structures industry, must issue the audit report on the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019). The auditor has the balance of the company as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), which is included below, and the following operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) to 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019).

**I.** The company has sold during the year 2.400 brackets at a price of 8 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 200 u.). A part of the sales of each month, always the same percentage, is charged in cash in the moment of the sale; the rest is payable to 90 days. Unfortunately the commercial department has lost the contract that fixes this percentage.

**II.** During the first quarter of 2019, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances of the previous year were paid. The customer debt outstanding from the previous year was charged in January, except 160 m.u. from an airline component maker declared in insolvency on 1 March 2019 (01/03/2019), which is definitively lost.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**III.** At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 800 kg of titanium bar valued at 1,50 m.u. / kg. On 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019) the company purchased 3.000 kg at 1,50 m.u. / kg, 50% payable to 60 days and the other 50% deferred until 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020). On 1 August 2019 (01/08/2019) it purchased 2.000 kg more at the same price, payable to 120 days. The count of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) shows 900 kg in the warehouse.

**IV.** Personnel expenses have been 400 m.u. / month (to which 120 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security); salaries are paid in the month in which they are produced and Social Security the month after. General expenses (electricity, insurance, cleaning) amount to 150 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

**V.** The machinery of the balance of 2018 was bought on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with residual value zero. On 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019) the company bought a 5-axis CNC centre that cost 4.800 m.u., paid in full in cash that day. To finance it, the same day a bank granted a loan of 3.600 m.u. at 5% annual interest, to be returned in one single payment on 1 April 2022 (01/04/2022); the interest is paid every 1 April for the year that ends that day. The CNC centre will be amortized linearly in 8 years with a residual value of 480 m.u.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**VI.** The long-term loan of the balance of 2018 bears 4% annual interest. The company returns 300 m.u. of principal every 30 June and every 31 December, paying the same days the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester.

**VII.** On 1 October 2019 (01/10/2019) the shareholders subscribed a capital increase of 500 new shares of 2 m.u. nominal value, without issue premium, disbursing that day only 50%; the rest will be called in 2020. On 15 November 2019 (15/11/2019) the company received in cash a dividend of 80 m.u. from its financial shares in AEROPIEZAS S.A., a permanent investment.

**VIII.** The bank statement at 23:00 hrs on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), before any operation of the closing, shows a balance of 3.024 m.u. The results are declared at 23:59 hrs; the corporation tax of 30% is paid immediately, and 50% of the profit after taxes is paid as dividends before the final balance at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019); the rest goes to reserves.

**BALANCE 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018)**

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**Required:**
1. Deduce, justifying it from the bank statement, the percentage of the sales that is charged in cash, and construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of TAHSA for the year 2019.
2. Construct and justify the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), showing all the intermediate calculations.
3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios in 2019.
4. The commercial director proposes for 2020 that 50% of the sales be charged in cash, granting on those cash sales a discount of 4%. Indicate what changes would have occurred in the Income Statement, the cash and the balance sheet of 2019 if this policy had been applied from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019). In which case is the profit higher, and in which case is the final cash balance higher? Discuss, reasoned, why.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**Unknown of the problem:** the share $p$ of each month's sales charged in cash. Every other flow of cash can be computed, so the bank statement before the closing (3.024 m.u.) gives one equation in $p$.

**Collections at 90 days:** a sale of January is collected in April; the sales of October, November and December are still pending at 31/12/2019.

**Uncalled capital:** the shareholders owe the 50% not yet disbursed; it is shown as a deduction of the subscribed capital, as in the Company X exercise of the course.

**Extension (not defined in the course decks).** $\text{ROA} = \text{Income from operations}/\text{Total assets}$ and $\text{ROE} = \text{Net profit}/\text{Owners equity}$, on the balance at 24:00 on 31/12/2019.

| **Total** | | **19.336** |

#### Step 2. Inflows other than the 2019 sales

$$\underbrace{1.600 - 160}_{\text{2018 receivables}} + \underbrace{3.600}_{\text{new loan}} + \underbrace{0{,}50 \times 1.000}_{\text{capital disbursed}} + \underbrace{80}_{\text{dividend received}} = 1.440 + 3.600 + 500 + 80 = 5.620 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 3. Equation for $p$

Monthly sales are $200 \times 8 = 1.600$ m.u. The cash part of every month is collected (12 months); the credit part only for January to September (9 months):

$$900 + 5.620 + 12 \times 1.600\,p + 9 \times 1.600\,(1 - p) - 19.336 = 3.024$$

$$19.200\,p + 14.400 - 14.400\,p = 3.024 + 19.336 - 900 - 5.620 = 15.840$$

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
$$4.800\,p = 15.840 - 14.400 = 1.440 \;\Rightarrow\; p = \frac{1.440}{4.800} = 0{,}30 = 30\%$$

Collections from 2019 sales: $19.200 \times 0{,}30 + 9 \times 1.120 = 5.760 + 10.080 = 15.840$ m.u.; pending at 31/12: $3 \times 1.120 = 3.360$ m.u.

#### Step 4. Titanium consumed

$$\text{Consumption} = 1.200 + 3.000 \times 1{,}50 + 2.000 \times 1{,}50 - 900 \times 1{,}50 = 1.200 + 4.500 + 3.000 - 1.350 = 7.350 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 5. Depreciation

$$D_{\text{machinery}} = \frac{6.000}{10} = 600 \quad \left(\text{check: } 3 \text{ years} \times 600 = 1.800 \text{ at } 31/12/2018 \;\checkmark\right)$$

$$D_{\text{CNC}} = \frac{4.800 - 480}{8} \times \frac{9}{12} = 540 \times \frac{9}{12} = 405, \qquad D_{2019} = 600 + 405 = 1.005 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 6. Financial items

$$I_{\text{old loan}} = 66 \text{ (Step 1)}, \qquad I_{\text{CNC loan}} = 3.600 \times 0{,}05 \times \frac{9}{12} = 135 \text{ (accrued, paid 01/04/2020)}$$

$$\text{Financial expenses} = 66 + 135 = 201, \qquad \text{Financial income (dividend received)} = 80 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 7. Income Statement 2019

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x: **Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the present policy**: the discount is a real cost of 384 m.u. (269 m.u. after tax). The **cash is higher with the new policy**: 576 m.u. more are collected in 2019 because more of each sale is charged at once, and the lower profit also means less tax and fewer dividends paid at the closing. The discount buys liquidity at the price of profitability; it is worth it only if the company needs the cash or if the money collected earlier earns more than the discount costs.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit, kg × m.u./kg and m.u./year × months/12 all give m.u.; $p$ and the ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why the bank balance is enough:** all the other flows are fixed by the terms of the contracts, so the cash balance determines the single unknown term, the share of cash sales.
- **Uncalled capital:** the 500 m.u. not disbursed are a debt of the shareholders to the company, not cash; showing them as a deduction keeps equity at the money actually contributed.
- **Typical mistakes:** paying the CNC loan interest in 2019, depreciating the CNC for 12 months, counting the dividend received as revenue from operations, and treating the bad debt as a collection.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
