chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: Bank B01 — NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The multiple-choice part is a practice format of the portal. Sources: 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf and 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercises 3 to 9; Examples PDF, Exercises 5 and 6; Topic 3, Slide 37.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.1 NPV of a two-year project
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q1
- concept_id: u3-npv-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: -120000+70000/1.05+80000/1.05**2

A project requires an initial outlay of 120,000 € and generates net cash flows of 70,000 € in year 1 and 80,000 € in year 2. With a yearly discount rate of 5%, its NPV is:

a) 30,000.00 €
b) 16,054.42 €
c) 19,229.02 €
d) 139,229.02 €

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Each flow is discounted to year 0 with its own exponent: $NPV = -120{,}000 + 70{,}000/1.05 + 80{,}000/1.05^2 = -120{,}000 + 66{,}666.67 + 72{,}562.36 = 19{,}229.02$ €.

- a) This is the undiscounted sum $70{,}000 + 80{,}000 - 120{,}000$, the NPV at 0%; the flows were not discounted.
- b) Both flows were divided by $1.05^2$: the year 1 flow was discounted twice instead of once.
- d) The present value of the inflows is right, but the initial outlay of 120,000 € was not subtracted.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.2 Largest outlay compatible with a given IRR
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q2
- concept_id: u3-max-outlay-from-irr
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 25000*(1/1.06+1/1.06**2+1/1.06**3)

A project is expected to generate 25,000 € at the end of each of the next three years, and its estimated IRR is 6%. The maximum amount that can be invested in it at year 0 is:

a) 66,825.30 €
b) 75,000.00 €
c) 70,754.72 €
d) 62,971.45 €

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
At the IRR the NPV is zero, so the outlay equals the present value of the flows at 6%: $I_0 = 25{,}000/1.06 + 25{,}000/1.06^2 + 25{,}000/1.06^3 = 23{,}584.91 + 22{,}249.91 + 20{,}990.48 = 66{,}825.30$ €.

- b) This is $3 \times 25{,}000$: the flows were added without discounting them at the IRR.
- c) The whole 75,000 € was discounted one year, as if every flow arrived at the end of year 1.
- d) The whole 75,000 € was discounted three years, as if every flow arrived at the end of year 3.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.3 Weighted average cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q3
- concept_id: u3-wacc-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 100*(0.35*0.12+0.65*0.05)

A company is financed 35% with equity, whose cost is estimated at 12%, and 65% with liabilities, whose average cost is 5%. Its capital cost $K_{WACC}$ is:

a) 8.50%
b) 9.55%
c) 17.00%
d) 7.45%

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
$K_{WACC} = K_{EQ}\,E/(E+L) + K_L\,L/(E+L) = 0.35 \times 12\% + 0.65 \times 5\% = 4.20\% + 3.25\% = 7.45\%$.

- a) This is the simple average $(12\% + 5\%)/2$; the costs were not weighted by the financial structure.
- b) The weights were swapped: $0.65 \times 12\% + 0.35 \times 5\%$ gives the equity cost the weight of the liabilities.
- c) The two costs were added, $12\% + 5\%$, which is not an average of any kind.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q4
- concept_id: u3-payback-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 2+(90000-30000-40000)/50000

A project requires 90,000 € and generates 30,000 €, 40,000 € and 50,000 € in years 1, 2 and 3. Assuming that each flow arrives evenly during its year, its payback period is:

a) 2.25 years
b) 2.40 years
c) 2.67 years
d) 3.00 years

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
After two years $30{,}000 + 40{,}000 = 70{,}000$ € are recovered; the remaining $90{,}000 - 70{,}000 = 20{,}000$ € come from the 50,000 € of year 3 after $20{,}000/50{,}000 = 0.40$ years, so the payback is 2.40 years.

- a) The outlay was divided by the average flow, $90{,}000/40{,}000$; the payback follows the cumulative flows year by year, not their average.
- c) The missing 20,000 € were divided by the year 1 flow (30,000 €) instead of the flow of year 3, the year in which the recovery happens.
- d) The recovery was rounded up to the end of year 3, ignoring that the flows arrive evenly during the year.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x: 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 5 (b) and Exercise 9 (a) (fraction of the year in which the outlay is recovered).

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q5
- concept_id: u3-fisher-rate-definition
- format: identify
- asks: definition

Fisher's rate of two investment projects is:

a) The discount rate at which the NPV of each project is zero
b) The weighted average of the costs of equity and liabilities of the company
c) The discount rate at which both projects have the same NPV
d) The discount rate at which each project recovers its initial outlay

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
The key of Exercise 9 obtains Fisher's rate from $NPV_A = NPV_B$; it is the rate at which the NPV profiles of the two projects cross, so the preferred project changes there.

- a) The rate that makes the NPV of one project zero is its IRR, a property of a single project, not of a pair.
- b) This is the capital cost $K_{WACC}$ of Slide 37, a property of the company's financing, not of two projects.
- d) The time in which a project recovers its outlay is the payback period, which is measured in years, not a discount rate.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.6 Both IRRs below the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q6
- concept_id: u3-irr-below-cost-of-capital
- format: what-happens
- asks: application

Two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 9.2% (project A) and 8.4% (project B). The company's cost of capital is 9.5%. Under the IRR criterion, the company should:

a) Undertake A, because it has the higher IRR
b) Undertake both, because both IRRs are positive
c) Undertake B, because its outlay is recovered with a lower rate
d) Reject both, because both IRRs are below the cost of capital

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
A project is accepted only when its IRR exceeds the cost of capital; here $9.2\% < 9.5\%$ and $8.4\% < 9.5\%$, so both NPVs at 9.5% are negative and neither project is undertaken, whatever their ranking.

- a) Ranking A above B is correct, but ranking alone does not make A acceptable: its IRR is still below the 9.5% cut-off rate.
- b) A positive IRR is not the acceptance condition; the IRR must exceed the cost of capital, and the projects are mutually exclusive anyway.
- c) A lower IRR makes a project less attractive, not more: this inverts the meaning of the IRR.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.7 Effect of a higher discount rate
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q7
- concept_id: u3-irr-npv-relation
- format: cause-effect
- asks: effect

A project made of an initial outlay followed by positive flows has an IRR of 12% and has been valued at 6%. If the discount rate is raised to 9%, its NPV:

a) Decreases, but remains positive
b) Increases, because the project earns more than 9%
c) Becomes negative, because the rate has risen
d) Does not change, because the IRR does not depend on the rate

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
The NPV of such a project falls as the rate rises, so it is lower at 9% than at 6%; since 9% is still below the 12% IRR, at which the NPV is zero, it remains positive. The key of Exercise 6 reasons the same way for rates of 7% and 9% with an IRR of 10%.

- b) A higher rate divides every future flow by a larger factor $(1+k)^t$, so the NPV cannot increase.
- c) The NPV becomes negative only when the rate exceeds the IRR (12%), not as soon as it rises.
- d) The IRR itself does not change, but the NPV is evaluated at the discount rate and does change with it.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.8 A false statement about payback
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q8
- concept_id: u3-payback-limits
- format: false-statement
- asks: comparison

Which one of the following statements about the payback period is FALSE:

a) It is the time it takes to recover the initial investment from the project's cash flows
b) Of two projects, the one with the shorter payback always has the higher NPV
c) It does not take into account the cash flows received after the outlay is recovered
d) A project accepted under a maximum payback of three years may have a negative NPV

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Payback and NPV can rank projects differently. In Exercise 9 of the sheet project B has the shorter payback (about 11 months against 1 year and 9 months), yet above Fisher's rate of about 5% project A has the higher NPV.

- a) True: this is the definition used in the key of Exercise 5 (b), so it is not the false statement asked for.
- c) True: payback stops counting when the outlay is recovered, which is why it ignores later flows; not the false one.
- d) True: in Exercise 5 project A has a payback of one year and an NPV of −90.91 € at 10%, so this statement is not false.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.9 IRR ranking against NPV at the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q9
- concept_id: u3-ranking-conflict
- format: identify
- asks: application

Two mutually exclusive projects: A has an IRR of 14% and B an IRR of 11%; B has the larger NPV at 0%, and their Fisher's rate is 7%. The company uses the NPV criterion with a cost of capital of 5%. It should choose:

a) A, because it has the higher IRR
b) Neither, because the IRRs disagree with the NPV at 0%
c) Both, because both IRRs exceed 5%
d) B, because below the Fisher's rate B has the higher NPV

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
The two NPV profiles cross only at Fisher's rate (7%). At 0% B has the larger NPV, so B stays above A for every rate below 7%; at 5% the NPV criterion chooses B, even though A has the higher IRR.

- a) The IRR ranking holds only above Fisher's rate; at 5% it disagrees with the NPV ranking, and the company decides by NPV.
- b) A disagreement between rankings does not make the projects unacceptable: both IRRs exceed 5%, so both NPVs are positive.
- c) The projects are mutually exclusive, so only one of them can be undertaken even if both are acceptable.

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.h: B01.10 The cost of each financial resource
chunks.x:
- id: B01-Q10
- concept_id: u3-cost-of-equity
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

In the capital cost of the company, equity has ... cost and liabilities have ... cost:

a) an implicit (opportunity) ... an explicit
b) no ... an explicit
c) an explicit ... an implicit (opportunity)
d) an explicit ... no

chunks.t: NPV, IRR, payback and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Slide 37 states that every financial resource has a cost: equity has an implicit (opportunity) cost and liabilities an explicit cost (the interest), and both enter the weighted average $K_{WACC}$.

- b) Equity is not free: the owners give up other uses of their funds, which is its opportunity cost.
- c) The two kinds of cost were swapped: interest on liabilities is the explicit one.
- d) Liabilities do carry a cost (their interest), and equity's cost is not explicit but implicit.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: Bank B02 — Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). Content: Topic 4 (The Production Function), Slides 7 to 42, and Exercise 1 of the examples PDF.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q1
- concept_id: u4-cost-classification
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A machining shop makes titanium brackets for aircraft seats. Which of the following costs is a variable cost:

a) The annual lease of the workshop
b) The salary of the plant manager
c) The titanium bar consumed by each bracket
d) The depreciation of the CNC machines

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
A variable cost grows with the volume produced, so total cost is $TC = FC + VC\,Q$ with $VC$ per unit (Topic 4, Slide 37). The titanium consumed by each bracket is spent once per unit, so it is a variable cost; the other three are paid whatever the volume, as the rent and the fixed staff costs of Exercise 1 of the examples PDF.

- a) The lease is paid in full whether the shop makes one bracket or ten thousand, so it is a fixed cost.
- b) A manager's salary does not depend on the number of brackets produced; it is a fixed cost of the period.
- d) The yearly depreciation of the machines is the same at any volume of output, so it belongs to the fixed costs.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q2
- concept_id: u4-bep-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 900000/(250-175)

A maker of avionics cooling fans has fixed costs of 900,000 € per year, sells each fan at 250 € and has a variable cost of 175 € per fan. Its break-even point is:

a) 12,000 units
b) 3,600 units
c) 5,143 units
d) 2,118 units

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
The unit margin is $m = P - VC = 250 - 175 = 75$ € per fan, and the break-even point is $Q_0 = FC/m = 900{,}000/75 = 12{,}000$ units (Topic 4, Slide 37).

- b) 3,600 units divides the fixed costs by the price, 900,000/250, forgetting that each unit must also pay its own variable cost.
- c) 5,143 units divides the fixed costs by the variable cost per unit, 900,000/175, which has no economic meaning.
- d) 2,118 units adds price and variable cost, 900,000/(250 + 175), instead of subtracting them to get the margin.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: B02.3 Break-even point with a commercial discount
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q3
- concept_id: u4-bep-commercial-discount
- format: numeric
- asks: application
- calc: 360000/(80*0.9-54)

A supplier of cabin LED strips has a list price of 80 € per unit and gives a 10% commercial discount on the list price to all its customers. Its variable cost is 54 € per unit and its fixed costs are 360,000 € per year. Its break-even point is:

a) 13,846 units
b) 15,385 units
c) 5,000 units
d) 20,000 units

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
Revenue is earned at the net price, $P = 0.90 \times 80 = 72$ € per unit, so $m = 72 - 54 = 18$ € and $Q_0 = 360{,}000/18 = 20{,}000$ units (Topic 4, Slide 37; the discount is handled as in Examples PDF, Exercise 1).

- a) 13,846 units uses the list price, 360,000/(80 − 54), as if no customer received the discount.
- b) 15,385 units applies the 10% discount to the margin, 360,000/(0.9 × 26), instead of to the price; the variable cost is not discounted.
- c) 5,000 units divides the fixed costs by the net price, 360,000/72, and forgets to subtract the variable cost.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: B02.4 Effect of a fall in sales
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q4
- concept_id: u4-operating-leverage-meaning
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

A drone maker has an operating leverage of 4 at its current volume. If its sales fall by 5%, what happens to its operating profit:

a) It falls by 1.25%
b) It falls by 20%
c) It falls by 5%, the same as the sales
d) It falls by 4%

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
$OL = (\Delta\text{Profit}/\text{Profit})/(\Delta Q/Q)$, so the relative change of the profit is $OL \times \Delta Q/Q = 4 \times (-5\%) = -20\%$ (Topic 4, Slides 39 and 40: with OL = 3 a 10% fall in sales lowers profit by 30%).

- a) 1.25% divides the change in sales by the leverage, inverting the ratio that defines the OL.
- c) A change equal to that of sales would mean OL = 1, which ignores the effect of the fixed costs.
- d) 4% reads the leverage itself as the change in profit, forgetting to multiply it by the 5% change in sales.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: B02.5 Leverage from the break-even point
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q5
- concept_id: u4-ol-from-bep
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 40000/(40000-30000)

A firm that makes oxygen masks for airliners has a break-even point of 30,000 units and sells 40,000 units. Its operating leverage is:

a) 0.25
b) 1.33
c) 4.00
d) 3.00

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
Since $FC = Q^*\,m$, the leverage depends only on the distance to the break-even point: $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*) = 40{,}000/(40{,}000 - 30{,}000) = 4$ (Topic 4, Slide 42). A 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 4%.

- a) 0.25 is $(Q - Q^*)/Q$, the inverse of the right ratio.
- b) 1.33 is $Q/Q^*$, which divides by the break-even volume instead of by the distance to it.
- d) 3.00 is $Q^*/(Q - Q^*)$, with the break-even volume in the numerator instead of the actual volume.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: B02.6 Leverage of a firm in losses
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q6
- concept_id: u4-ol-losses
- format: true-statement
- asks: definition

A firm sells fewer units than its break-even point ($Q < Q^*$). Which one of the following statements about its operating leverage is TRUE:

a) It is greater than 1, so profit reacts more than proportionally to sales
b) It lies between 0 and 1, because the firm is in losses
c) It equals 1, because the fixed costs are not covered
d) It is zero or negative, and below −1 it amplifies the effect of a change in sales

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
With $Q < Q^*$ the denominator of $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ is negative, so $OL \le 0$; for $OL < -1$ the effect is more than proportional (amplifier) and for $-1 < OL < 0$ it is less than proportional (Topic 4, Slide 42).

- a) OL greater than 1 is the case of a firm with profits ($Q > Q^*$), not of a firm in losses.
- b) No volume gives an OL between 0 and 1: above the break-even point OL > 1 and below it OL ≤ 0.
- c) OL = 1 would need zero fixed costs; at the break-even point itself the leverage is not even defined.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q7
- concept_id: u4-production-system-types
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A company builds satellite ground stations. Each station is designed for one client, and machinery, materials and workers are brought to the site where it is built. Its type of production and plant layout are:

a) Project production with a fixed layout
b) Batch production with a functional layout
c) Mass production with a product layout
d) Continuous production with a product layout

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
Individualized products with qualified workers and difficult planning are the project type, and a product that stays in one place while resources are brought to it is the fixed layout (Topic 4, Slides 7, 23 and 26).

- b) Batch production makes a variety of products in batches in a functional layout; it does not build a single one-off unit on site.
- c) Mass production makes standard products for mass markets along a line, the opposite of a design for one client.
- d) Continuous production (petrochemistry) is the high-volume end of the product-process matrix, with no individualized product.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q8
- concept_id: u4-just-in-time
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Which of the following is a mechanism of visual control of Just in Time production:

a) Poka Yoke
b) Job cells
c) Kanban
d) U-shaped plant distribution

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
The course lists Andon, control panels, work sheets and Kanban as the mechanisms of visual control of Just in Time (Topic 4, Slide 21).

- a) Poka Yoke is listed, with Jidoka, as a mechanism to support quality, not of visual control.
- b) Job cells are the tool of internal organization of Just in Time, not a visual control.
- d) The U shape is the plant distribution of Just in Time, not a mechanism of visual control.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q9
- concept_id: u4-total-productivity
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 540000/(120000+90000+150000+40000)

In one month a workshop that repairs aircraft wheels produces services worth 540,000 €. It uses labour worth 120,000 €, capital worth 90,000 €, raw materials worth 150,000 € and energy worth 40,000 €. Its total productivity index is:

a) 4.50
b) 0.74
c) 2.57
d) 1.35

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
Total productivity divides goods and services by all the factors together: $540{,}000/(120{,}000 + 90{,}000 + 150{,}000 + 40{,}000) = 540{,}000/400{,}000 = 1.35$ (Topic 4, Slide 34).

- a) 4.50 is 540,000/120,000, the labour productivity: a partial index, not the total one.
- b) 0.74 is 400,000/540,000, inputs over outputs, the inverse of the index.
- c) 2.57 divides only by labour and capital, 540,000/210,000, leaving out raw materials and energy.

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.h: B02.10 Fixed costs and economic risk
chunks.x:
- id: B02-Q10
- concept_id: u4-fixed-costs-economic-risk
- format: cause-effect
- asks: comparison

Two firms of the same sector sell the same number of units and earn the same operating profit, but firm A has higher fixed costs than firm B. Which one of the following is TRUE:

a) Both have the same operating leverage, because they earn the same profit
b) Firm A has the higher operating leverage and therefore the higher economic risk
c) Firm B has the higher operating leverage, because its variable costs are higher
d) Firm A has the lower economic risk, because its fixed costs do not change with sales

chunks.t: Break-even point, operating leverage and production
chunks.x:
$OL = Q\,m/\text{Profit}$. With the same profit, $Q\,m = \text{Profit} + FC$ is larger for the firm with higher fixed costs, so firm A has the higher OL; the OL is an index of economic (operating) risk and, ceteris paribus, higher fixed costs give a higher OL (Topic 4, Slides 39 and 41).

- a) Equal profits do not give equal leverage: the numerator $Q\,m$ also contains the fixed costs, which differ.
- c) Higher variable costs mean a smaller margin and smaller $Q\,m$ for the same profit, so firm B has the lower OL.
- d) Fixed costs that do not change with sales are exactly what makes profit more sensitive to sales, so A carries more risk, not less.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: Bank B03 — Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong). The examples PDF has no multiple-choice part: this is a practice format of the portal. Content: Topic 5, Slides 7-8, 10, 17, 20, 24, 31 and 37; topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-3; PED Exercises SOL.pdf, Exercises 1-4.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.1 A phase of the analysis system
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q1
- concept_id: u5-strategic-marketing-phases
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Which one of the following is a phase of strategic marketing, and not of operative marketing:

a) Establishing the marketing budget
b) Diagnosing the situation with a SWOT analysis
c) Controlling and assessing the results of the marketing mix
d) Executing the marketing-mix strategies

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
Strategic marketing has four stages: analysis of the situation, diagnosis of the situation with a SWOT analysis, definition of the marketing objective, and formulation of the strategies (segmentation and positioning). The SWOT diagnosis is its second stage.

- a) Establishing the marketing budget is part of the action plan of the marketing mix, the first stage of operative marketing.
- c) Control and assessment is the third stage of operative marketing, which checks the execution of the marketing mix.
- d) Executing the marketing-mix strategies is the second stage of operative marketing, the action system, not the analysis system.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q2
- concept_id: u5-pe-initial-base
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: ((1700 - 2000) / 2000) / ((440 - 400) / 400)

A maker of drone batteries raises the price of its main model from 400 m.u. to 440 m.u., and its monthly sales fall from 2,000 to 1,700 units. Taking the percentage changes with respect to the initial values, as on Slide 17, the coefficient of price elasticity of demand (with its sign) is:

a) −0.67
b) −1.70
c) −1.50
d) −1.94

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
With the initial values as the base, $\%\Delta Q = (1{,}700 - 2{,}000)/2{,}000 = -15\%$ and $\%\Delta P = (440 - 400)/400 = +10\%$, so $E_d = -15\%/10\% = -1.50$. Its absolute value, 1.5, is above 1: the demand is elastic.

- a) −0.67 is the price change divided by the quantity change, the ratio turned upside down.
- b) −1.70 uses the midpoints of the interval (1,850 units and 420 m.u.) as the base, which the question does not ask for.
- d) −1.94 takes the final values (1,700 units and 440 m.u.) as the base instead of the initial ones.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.3 Sales after a price rise
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q3
- concept_id: u5-pe-quantity-forecast
- format: numeric
- asks: application
- calc: 12000 * (1 - 0.8 * 0.15)

A supplier of cabin headsets sells 12,000 units a year. The price elasticity of demand is 0.8 in absolute value, and the firm raises its price by 15%. With the percentage changes taken with respect to the initial values, the expected yearly sales are:

a) $10{,}560$ units
b) $13{,}440$ units
c) $9{,}750$ units
d) $10{,}200$ units

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
From $E_d = \%\Delta Q/\%\Delta P$ with the sign of the law of demand, $\%\Delta Q = (-0.8) \times 15\% = -12\%$. The new sales are $12{,}000 \times (1 - 0.12) = 10{,}560$ units: the demand is inelastic, so the quantity falls by less, in percentage, than the price rises.

- b) 13,440 units adds the 12% instead of subtracting it: the negative sign of the elasticity (law of demand) has been ignored.
- c) 9,750 units divides the price change by the elasticity ($15\%/0.8 = 18.75\%$) instead of multiplying them.
- d) 10,200 units applies the 15% price change to the quantity, as if the elasticity were 1 (unit elastic demand).

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.4 Midpoint elasticity of an interval
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q4
- concept_id: u5-pe-midpoint
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: ((420 - 300) / ((420 + 300) / 2)) / ((40 - 50) / ((40 + 50) / 2))

On the demand table of a satellite-imagery service, a price of 50 m.u. per image goes with 300 images a week and a price of 40 m.u. with 420 images. The price elasticity of demand at the midpoint of this interval, computed as in Exercise 1 of the course's elasticity sheet, is:

a) −2.00
b) −1.14
c) −0.67
d) −1.50

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
The midpoint method divides each change by the average of its two values: $\bar Q = (300 + 420)/2 = 360$ and $\bar P = (50 + 40)/2 = 45$. Then $\Delta Q/\bar Q = 120/360 = 0.3333$ and $\Delta P/\bar P = -10/45 = -0.2222$, so $E_d = 0.3333/(-0.2222) = -1.50$.

- a) −2.00 takes the initial values (300 images, 50 m.u.) as the base, the simple formula of Slide 17, not the midpoint asked for.
- b) −1.14 takes the final values (420 images, 40 m.u.) as the base.
- c) −0.67 is the midpoint ratio turned upside down: price change over quantity change.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.5 Cutting the price with inelastic demand
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q5
- concept_id: u5-elasticity-income
- format: cause-effect
- asks: effect

A training-simulator firm faces a price elasticity of demand of 0.6 in absolute value and cuts its price by 10%. What happens to its income from sales:

a) It rises, because the quantity sold rises by more, in percentage, than the price falls
b) It falls, because the quantity sold rises by about 6%, less than the 10% fall of the price
c) It does not change, because the rise in quantity exactly offsets the fall in price
d) It falls, because the quantity sold falls by about 6% together with the price

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
With $\lvert E_d \rvert = 0.6 < 1$ the demand is inelastic: a 10% price cut raises the quantity by about $0.6 \times 10\% = 6\%$. Income $I = P \cdot Q$ is multiplied by about $0.90 \times 1.06 = 0.954$, a fall of about 4.6%.

- a) This is what happens with elastic demand ($\lvert E_d \rvert > 1$), not with an elasticity of 0.6.
- c) Income stays the same only with unit elastic demand ($\lvert E_d \rvert = 1$).
- d) The law of demand makes the quantity rise when the price falls; this option has the wrong sign of the elasticity.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.6 A new line in a cabin-interiors range
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q6
- concept_id: u5-range-characteristics
- format: what-happens
- asks: application

A cabin-interiors firm offers three product lines: seats (4 models), galleys (3 models) and lavatories (2 models). It now launches a fourth line, cabin lighting, with 2 models. What happens to its range of products:

a) Only the depth increases, because the firm now offers more individual products
b) Only the length increases; the extension stays at three because lighting is also a cabin product
c) The extension (width) rises from 3 to 4 lines and the length from 9 to 11 products; the depth of the existing lines does not change
d) The consistency of the range is lost, because every new line lowers the consistency with the final use

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
The extension, or width (breadth), of the range is the number of product lines (3 to 4); the length is the total number of individual products ($4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ to $9 + 2 = 11$). The depth is the number of products per line, so the existing lines keep 4, 3 and 2 models. Adding a line is the strategy "add more product lines".

- a) Depth counts products per line; the existing lines gain no models, so their depth does not change.
- b) A new line raises the extension whatever its use; lines are counted, not grouped by the market they serve.
- d) Consistency refers to the final use of the products; lighting is still used in the aircraft cabin, so the range stays consistent.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.7 Segmenting by how often customers fly
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q7
- concept_id: u5-segmentation-criteria
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A regional airline divides its passengers into regular flyers and occasional flyers and designs a different offer for each group. Which segmentation criterion is it using:

a) Psychological and purchase behaviour
b) Demographic
c) Geographical
d) Price-quality relationship

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
The frequency of purchase (regular or temporary) is listed under the psychological and purchase-behaviour criteria, together with personality, lifestyle and the type of use of the product.

- b) Demographic criteria are age, sex, family size, level of income and type of job, not how often a person buys.
- c) Geographical criteria are national, international, regional or different areas, not the frequency of purchase.
- d) The price-quality relationship is a basis for positioning a product, not a criterion for dividing the market into segments.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q8
- concept_id: u5-brand-types
- format: false-statement
- asks: definition

Which one of the following statements about the brand is FALSE:

a) The name is the part of the brand that can be said
b) The logo includes the design, symbol, graph and distinct colours of the brand
c) A family (umbrella) brand places one name over many products or businesses
d) A dealer brand is owned by the manufacturer that produces the goods

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
A dealer brand is owned by a wholesaler or a retailer, not by the manufacturer; the brand owned by the producer is the manufacturer brand.

- a) This is how Slide 20 defines the name, so the statement is true.
- b) Slide 20 defines the logo as design, symbol, graph and distinct colours, so the statement is true.
- c) Slide 21 shows umbrella branding as one name over many businesses, so the statement is true.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.h: B03.9 One authorised centre per region
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q9
- concept_id: u5-distribution-intensity
- format: identify
- asks: application

A maker of business-jet engines sells its overhaul kits through only one authorised service centre in each region, and that centre may not carry competing brands. Which distribution strategy is this:

a) Intensive distribution
b) Selective distribution
c) Exclusive distribution
d) A direct channel, because the producer controls who sells the kits

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
Slide 37 names three distribution strategies: intensive, selective and exclusive. Extension (definitions not given on the slide): intensive distribution uses as many outlets as possible, selective distribution uses a limited number of chosen outlets per area, and exclusive distribution grants one outlet per area the sole right to sell the product, often without competing brands. One centre per region with no competing brands is exclusive.

- a) Intensive distribution would place the kits in as many outlets as possible, the opposite of one centre per region.
- b) Selective distribution chooses several outlets per area; here the producer allows only one.
- d) The service centres are independent intermediaries, so the channel is indirect; a direct channel has the producer selling to the final buyer.

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
- id: B03-Q10
- concept_id: u5-promotion-mix
- format: identify
- asks: classification

During the first three months after launching a new agricultural drone, the maker offers 20% off its maintenance kits to every buyer. Which activity of the promotion mix is this:

a) Advertising
b) Sales promotion
c) Public relations
d) Personal selling

chunks.t: Marketing mix, segmentation and price elasticity
chunks.x:
Sales promotion is any activity that offers an incentive for a limited period to induce a desired response from customers; the discount does not ordinarily come with the product.

- a) Advertising is a paid form of non-personal communication through the mass media by an identified sponsor; it carries a message, not an incentive.
- c) Public relations build and keep a favourable image of the firm with its stakeholders, through the media or sponsorship, not through discounts.
- d) Personal selling is a person-to-person process in which a seller learns the buyer's wants; no salesperson is involved here.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: Bank B04 — Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The multiple-choice part is a practice format of the portal: the examples PDF has none. Content: Topic 6, Slides 5-6, 8-10, 12, 15, 18 and 22-24.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: B04.1 Steps 3 to 6 of the decision-making process
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q1
- concept_id: u6-decision-process-order
- format: ordering
- asks: definition

Which sequence gives steps 3 to 6 of the decision-making process in the order of the course?

a) Analysing the alternatives, considering alternative courses of action, choosing an alternative, implementing the decision
b) Considering alternative courses of action, analysing the alternatives, choosing an alternative, implementing the decision
c) Considering alternative courses of action, choosing an alternative, analysing the alternatives, implementing the decision
d) Gathering information, considering alternative courses of action, choosing an alternative, evaluating the results

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
The eight steps are: recognizing the problem or opportunity, gathering information, considering alternative courses of action, analysing the alternatives, choosing an alternative, implementing the decision, evaluating the results and implementing changes. Steps 3 to 6 are therefore option b.

- a) The alternatives cannot be analysed before they have been considered (generated): step 3 comes before step 4.
- c) Choosing before analysing inverts steps 4 and 5; the choice must rest on the analysis of the alternatives.
- d) Gathering information is step 2 and evaluating the results is step 7, so this list skips the analysis and the implementation.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: B04.2 A known fault with a written procedure
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q2
- concept_id: u6-decision-types
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A hangar supervisor meets a hydraulic leak that is well known to the team, and the maintenance manual gives the approved repair. Which type of decision does the supervisor take?

a) An innovative decision
b) An adaptable decision
c) A strategic decision
d) A routine (planned) decision

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
The problem is known and well defined and the alternative solution is known in advance (the manual), which is the definition of a routine, planned decision.

- a) An innovative decision faces an unusual, ambiguous problem with unplanned alternatives, which is not the case of a fault the manual already covers.
- b) An adaptable decision lies between the two extremes, for a problem or alternatives only partly known; here both are fully known.
- c) Strategic classifies a decision by management level (top management), not by the type of problem and alternatives, and a single repair is not a strategic matter.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: B04.3 Presenting the results to the press
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q3
- concept_id: u6-mintzberg-roles
- format: identify
- asks: classification

At an air show, the CEO of a satellite manufacturer explains the firm's yearly results and plans to journalists. Which managerial role of Mintzberg does the CEO play?

a) Spokesperson, an informational role
b) Negotiator, a decisional role
c) Resource allocator, a decisional role
d) Leader, an interpersonal role

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Transmitting information about the firm to people outside it is the spokesperson role, one of the three informational roles (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson). The slide lists the roles by name only; the meaning used here is the usual one of Mintzberg's classification.

- b) The negotiator role means bargaining with another party (a supplier, a union); giving information to the press involves no negotiation.
- c) The resource allocator decides how money, people and time are distributed inside the firm, which is not what a press briefing does.
- d) The leader role concerns motivating and directing the firm's own employees, while here the audience is outside the firm.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q4
- concept_id: u6-managerial-skills
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

Complete the sentence: "The ability to understand how things operate, which weighs most in low management, is the ______ skill."

a) conceptual
b) interpersonal
c) technical
d) decisional

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
The course defines the technical skill as the ability to understand how things operate; its share is largest for first-line supervisors and smallest for top management.

- a) The conceptual skill is the ability to see the firm as a whole, and it weighs most in top management, not in low management.
- b) The interpersonal skill is the ability to interact with people at work successfully, needed at every level of the hierarchy.
- d) Decisional is a group of Mintzberg's managerial roles, not one of the three basic managerial skills.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q5
- concept_id: u6-professional-bureaucracy
- format: false-statement
- asks: definition

Which statement about the professional bureaucracy is false?

a) It relies on high horizontal specialization with highly qualified employees.
b) It coordinates through the standardization of outputs, skills and knowledge.
c) It concentrates decision-making power at the strategic apex.
d) It suits big organizations in a stable but complex environment.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
The professional bureaucracy is decentralized: qualified professionals of the operating core decide on their own work, and the staff mainly supports that core. Centralized power belongs to the machine bureaucracy (and direct supervision by the apex to the simple structure).

- a) This statement is true: high horizontal specialization with highly qualified employees is listed as a feature of the configuration.
- b) This statement is true: standardization of outputs, skills and knowledge is how the professionals are coordinated.
- d) This statement is true: the configuration is that of big organizations in a stable but complex environment.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: B04.6 Talking past the organization chart
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q6
- concept_id: u6-formal-informal-structure
- format: what-happens
- asks: application

The organization chart of a drone maker says that problems between the design and the test departments go through the two department heads. In practice, the engineers of both departments solve them by talking directly at the coffee machine. What does this illustrate?

a) An informal structure, which together with the formal structure forms the real structure of the firm
b) A change of the formal structure, because management has redrawn the organization chart
c) Centralization of decision-making in the two department heads
d) The creation of a technostructure that designs new processes

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Informal contacts, communications and ways of doing things that employees develop on their own are the informal structure; combined with the formal structure defined by management, they give the real structure.

- b) The formal structure is defined by management, and in the case management has changed nothing: the chart still prescribes the old route.
- c) The engineers bypass the heads, so decisions are taken lower down, which is the opposite of centralization.
- d) The technostructure is a formal part made of analysts who design systems and processes, not a spontaneous habit of engineers.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q7
- concept_id: u6-simple-structure
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A start-up of three people builds CubeSat components. The founder assigns and checks the work of the two engineers directly; there are no middle managers, analysts or support departments. Which basic configuration does it have?

a) Adhocracy
b) Machine bureaucracy
c) Division organization
d) Simple structure

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Only a strategic apex (the founder) and an operating core (the engineers), coordination by direct supervision of the apex, and a start-up or very small business: these are the features of the simple structure.

- a) An adhocracy mixes middle line, operating core and staff in a matrix of experts and is used as a complementary structure for specific projects; here there is no middle line or staff to mix.
- b) A machine bureaucracy needs many rules, many hierarchical layers and a big, mature organization, the opposite of a three-person firm.
- c) A division organization requires autonomous divisions led by a middle line, which a firm with no middle managers cannot have.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q8
- concept_id: u6-recruitment-selection
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

Complete the sentence: "Within human resources management, ______ attracts candidates to the firm and comes before ______, which chooses among them."

a) selection ... recruitment
b) recruitment ... selection
c) training ... performance appraisal
d) compensation ... recruitment

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Human resources management is the process of recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and compensating employees, in that order. Recruitment attracts candidates and selection then chooses among them.

- a) This inverts the two activities: selection cannot choose among candidates who have not yet been attracted by recruitment.
- c) Training and performance appraisal act on people already hired, so neither attracts or chooses candidates.
- d) Compensation rewards employees already in the firm, and recruitment comes first in the process, not after compensation.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q9
- concept_id: u6-controlling
- format: ordering
- asks: definition

Which list gives the activities of controlling in the order of the course?

a) Establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations, taking corrective action if required
b) Measuring actual performance, establishing standards, taking corrective action, identifying deviations
c) Developing forecasts, defining strategic objectives, developing alternative courses of action, deciding on a course of action
d) Recognizing the problem, gathering information, choosing an alternative, evaluating the results

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
Controlling ensures that activities provide the planned results: a standard is set first, actual performance is measured against it, deviations are identified and corrective action is taken if required.

- b) Performance cannot be judged before a standard exists, and corrective action presupposes that a deviation has been identified first.
- c) These are the four main steps of planning, the function that sets the goals controlling later checks.
- d) These are steps of the decision-making process, not the activities of controlling.

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.h: B04.10 Why an adhocracy for a prototype project
chunks.x:
- id: B04-Q10
- concept_id: u6-adhocracy
- format: cause-effect
- asks: cause

An aircraft manufacturer sets up a team of designers, test engineers and suppliers' specialists to build an eVTOL demonstrator in eighteen months, organized as an adhocracy. Why does that configuration suit the project?

a) Because its high standardization and formalization reduce the errors of a new design
b) Because it concentrates every decision in the strategic apex, which speeds up approvals
c) Because its low standardization and formalization, decentralized decisions and matrix departmentalization give the flexibility an innovative project needs
d) Because its many hierarchical layers and low span of control keep a close check on each specialist

chunks.t: Roles, configurations and people
chunks.x:
The adhocracy has high horizontal and low vertical specialization, low standardization and formalization, decentralization as the key to flexibility and matrix departmentalization, and it is used as a complementary structure for specific projects, which is the situation of the demonstrator.

- a) High standardization and formalization describe the machine bureaucracy; in the adhocracy both are low and the technostructure disappears.
- b) Centralization in the apex is the feature of the simple structure and of the machine bureaucracy; the adhocracy is decentralized.
- d) Many layers and a low span of control are features of the machine bureaucracy, which would slow down an innovative project.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: Bank B05 — Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The examples PDF has no multiple-choice part and no Topic 7 exercise; content from Topic 7, Slides 4, 6, 9 and 11-19.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.1 The most important source of innovation
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q1
- concept_id: u7-sources-linkages
- format: identify
- asks: definition

According to the course, which is the most important source of innovation:

a) The lone individual inventor working on a problem of his or her own
b) The linkages between individuals, firms, universities, government-funded research and private non-profit organizations
c) The central corporate research laboratories of large firms
d) Government laboratories, science parks and incubators

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Topic 7, Slide 4: the most important source of innovation is the linkages between the players; networks of innovators that leverage knowledge and other resources from multiple sources are one of the most powerful agents of technological advance.

- a) The individual inventor is one of the sources listed on Slide 3, but the course does not rank it first; it singles out the linkages between all the sources.
- c) Central corporate research ranks first among firms' sources of research work on Slide 6, which is a ranking inside firms, not the most important source of innovation overall.
- d) Government laboratories, science parks and incubators are one source among several (Slide 8), not the linkages that the course names as the most important source.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.2 First source of development work
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q2
- concept_id: u7-firm-rd-sources
- format: identify
- asks: classification

In the ranking of the sources of development work reported by firms (Roberts, 2001), which source comes first:

a) Central corporate research
b) Suppliers' technology
c) Sponsored university research
d) Internal R&D within divisions

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Slide 6 gives two rankings. For development work the first source is internal R&D within divisions, followed by central corporate research and suppliers' technology.

- a) Central corporate research is first for research work but second for development work; the option swaps the two rankings.
- b) Suppliers' technology is third in the ranking of development work, behind the two internal sources of the firm.
- c) Sponsored university research appears third in the ranking of research work and does not appear among the first sources of development work.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q3
- concept_id: u7-technological-spillovers
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

A positive externality of R&D that results from the spread of knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries is called ...

a) a technological spillover
b) a technology cluster
c) absorptive capacity
d) a network externality

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Topic 7, Slide 9 defines technological spillovers as a positive externality of R&D resulting from the spread of knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries.

- b) A technology cluster is a regional group of firms connected to a common technology, a set of firms, not the externality that flows between them.
- c) Absorptive capacity is the ability of an organization to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge (Slide 18), a capability of one firm, not a spread of knowledge.
- d) A network externality is the rise in the value of a good to a user as the number of its users grows (Slide 19); it is not caused by spread R&D knowledge.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.4 Robotic welding on the seat line
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q4
- concept_id: u7-product-vs-process
- format: identify
- asks: application

An aircraft-seat manufacturer installs robotic welding on its assembly line. The defect rate of the seat frames halves and the number of seats produced per shift rises by 20%, while the seats delivered to airlines are identical to the previous ones. Which type of innovation is this:

a) A product innovation, because the seats are the firm's output
b) An architectural innovation, because the assembly line is a system
c) A process innovation
d) A dominant design of the seat industry

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Process innovations change the way an organization conducts its business, such as the techniques of producing goods, and are often aimed at improving the effectiveness or efficiency of production by reducing defect rates or increasing the quantity produced in a given time, exactly what the robotic welding does (Slide 11).

- a) A product innovation is embodied in the outputs; here the seats delivered are unchanged, so the novelty is not in the output.
- b) Architectural innovation refers to a change in the overall design of a system and in how its components interact; nothing in the case changes the design of the seat or its configuration.
- d) A dominant design is a product or process architecture that holds usually 50% or more of a market, not a single firm's improvement of its own line.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q5
- concept_id: u7-competence-perspective
- format: false-statement
- asks: comparison

Which one of the following statements about competence-enhancing and competence-destroying innovations is FALSE:

a) Whether an innovation is competence-enhancing or competence-destroying depends on whose perspective is taken
b) A radical innovation is always competence-destroying for every firm of the industry
c) An innovation is competence-enhancing for a firm if it builds on that firm's existing knowledge base
d) An innovation is competence-destroying for a firm if it renders that firm's competencies obsolete

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
The statement is false because the course classifies competence effects firm by firm: the same innovation can enhance the competences of one firm and destroy those of another (Slide 12). Being radical (very new and different from prior solutions) is a different pair of the classification and does not fix the effect on every firm.

- a) True: Slide 12 states that the classification depends on whose perspective is being taken.
- c) True: this is the course's definition of competence-enhancing from the perspective of a particular firm.
- d) True: this is the course's definition of competence-destroying, which also covers an innovation that does not build on the firm's competences.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.6 From one rotor to four
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q6
- concept_id: u7-architectural-vs-component
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A drone maker moves from a single-rotor helicopter layout to a quadcopter. It keeps the same type of electric motors, batteries and cameras, but rearranges them and changes how they work together: the drone is now steered by varying the speed of four rotors instead of tilting the blades of one rotor. On the architectural vs component pair, this is ...

a) an architectural innovation, because it changes the overall design of the system and the way its components interact
b) a component innovation, because it changes one or more components without affecting the overall configuration
c) a component innovation, because the motors, batteries and cameras are of the same type as before
d) neither, because no new component has been invented

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Slide 13: an architectural innovation changes the overall design of a system or the way its components interact with each other. The layout and the control of the drone change, even though the components are of the same type.

- b) The definition is the right one for a component innovation, but the overall configuration of the drone does change, so it does not apply here.
- c) Reusing the same type of components is compatible with an architectural innovation; what matters is the change in configuration and interaction.
- d) An architectural innovation needs no new component: rearranging existing components into a new design is precisely what it covers.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.7 Doubling effort on a mature technology
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q7
- concept_id: u7-s-curve-limit
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

The technology of a firm is already in the flat upper part of its S-curve of performance. If the firm doubles the effort it invests in that technology, what happens to performance:

a) It improves faster than ever, because the steepest part of the curve lies at the top
b) It doubles, because performance is proportional to effort
c) It falls, because the curve turns down after its maximum
d) It improves only a little, because the technology is approaching its limit

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
On the S-curve of technology performance (Slide 14), performance improves slowly, then quickly, and then flattens as it approaches the limit of the technology; near that limit additional effort brings small gains.

- a) The steepest part of the S-curve is in the middle, not at the top, where the curve is flat.
- b) Performance is not proportional to effort: the curve is S-shaped, not a straight line through the origin.
- c) The S-curve does not turn down: it levels off at the limit of the technology drawn as a horizontal dotted line.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.8 Arrival of a discontinuous technology
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q8
- concept_id: u7-discontinuous-technology
- format: true-statement
- asks: comparison

Which one of the following statements about the introduction of a discontinuous technology is TRUE:

a) It always starts with a higher performance than the technology it replaces
b) It improves the components of the existing technology on the same knowledge base
c) It may start below the existing technology on its S-curve and later overtake it
d) It is the moment at which the diffusion of the existing technology reaches the laggards

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
A discontinuous technology fulfils a similar market need by building on an entirely new knowledge base; the technology S-curves of Slide 15 show that the second technology may start below the first one and later cross it.

- a) Slide 15 (b) draws the second technology below the first at the beginning, so "always higher" contradicts the course figure.
- b) Building on the same knowledge base describes an improvement of the existing technology, the opposite of an entirely new knowledge base.
- d) The laggards are the last adopter category of the diffusion curve (Slide 16), a pattern of adoption over time, not the definition of a discontinuous technology.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.h: B05.9 Young, well educated and risk-oriented
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q9
- concept_id: u7-adopter-categories
- format: identify
- asks: definition

Which adopter category is described as a larger but still small group (13.5%) of risk-oriented individuals, highly adaptable to new technology, who follow the innovators and tend to be young and well educated:

a) Early adopters
b) Innovators
c) Early majority
d) Late majority

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Slide 16 describes the early adopters as a larger but still relatively small group, risk-oriented and highly adaptable to new technology, who follow the innovators and tend to be young and well educated; they are 13.5% of the population.

- b) Innovators are the first 2.5%: leading-edge individuals extremely interested in technology, who come before the early adopters, not after them.
- c) The early majority (34%) is much larger and more careful, waiting to see how new ideas are received before investing.
- d) The late majority (34%) is slightly conservative and risk-averse and needs convincing, not risk-oriented.

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
- id: B05-Q10
- concept_id: u7-dominant-design-selection
- format: cause-effect
- asks: cause

Which pair of forces does the course give as the reasons why an industry selects a dominant design:

a) Official enforcement by a standards body and patent protection
b) Learning effects and network externalities
c) Technological spillovers and technology clusters
d) Product innovations and process innovations

chunks.t: Sources of innovation, innovation types and design dominance
chunks.x:
Slides 18-19: learning effects (the more a technology is used, the more it is developed and the more efficient it becomes) and network externalities (the value to a user grows with the number of users, through the installed base and complementary goods) push the market towards a single design, which can produce winner-take-all markets.

- a) A dominant design is a de facto standard: it need not be officially enforced (Slide 17), and patents are not among the reasons the course gives.
- c) Spillovers and clusters describe how innovation arises in collaborative networks (Slide 9), not why one design comes to dominate a market.
- d) Product and process are a pair of types of innovation (Slide 11); they classify innovations and do not explain the selection of a design.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: Bank B06 — Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The multiple-choice part is a practice format of the portal. Sources: 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf and 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercises 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9; Examples PDF, Exercises 5 and 6; Topic 3, Slide 37.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.1 NPV of a three-year project
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q1
- concept_id: u3-npv-three-year
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: -50000+20000/1.06+25000/1.06**2+15000/1.06**3

An avionics test bench costs 50,000 € today and will bring in 20,000 € at the end of year 1, 25,000 € at the end of year 2 and a final 15,000 € at the end of year 3, after which it is scrapped with no further flows. Valued at 6% a year, the bench is worth today, net of its cost:

a) 10,000.00 €
b) 3,712.12 €
c) 6,603.77 €
d) 4,467.78 €

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Each flow is discounted with the exponent of its own year: $NPV = -50{,}000 + 20{,}000/1.06 + 25{,}000/1.06^2 + 15{,}000/1.06^3 = -50{,}000 + 18{,}867.92 + 22{,}249.91 + 12{,}594.29 = 3{,}712.12$ €.

- a) This is $20{,}000 + 25{,}000 + 15{,}000 - 50{,}000$, the NPV at 0%: none of the flows was discounted.
- c) The whole 60,000 € was discounted one year, as if every flow arrived at the end of year 1.
- d) The year 3 flow was divided by $1.06^2$ instead of $1.06^3$, so it was discounted one year too few.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.2 IRR of a two-year project
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q2
- concept_id: u3-irr-two-year-quadratic
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 100*((150000+sqrt(150000**2+4*400000*330000))/(2*400000)-1)

A project requires 400,000 € and generates 150,000 € in year 1 and 330,000 € in year 2. Its IRR is:

a) 20.00%
b) 10.00%
c) 9.54%
d) 11.49%

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
With $x = 1 + r$, $-400{,}000 + 150{,}000/x + 330{,}000/x^2 = 0$ becomes $400{,}000x^2 - 150{,}000x - 330{,}000 = 0$, so $x = \left(150{,}000 + \sqrt{150{,}000^2 + 4 \times 400{,}000 \times 330{,}000}\right)/800{,}000 = (150{,}000 + 741{,}956.87)/800{,}000 = 1.1149$ and the IRR is 11.49%.

- a) This is $(480{,}000 - 400{,}000)/400{,}000$, the undiscounted gain over the outlay; it ignores that the flows arrive over two years.
- b) The 20% gain was spread evenly over the two years, a simple average that does not cancel the NPV.
- c) Both flows were treated as if they arrived in year 2, $x^2 = 480{,}000/400{,}000$, which discounts the year 1 flow one year too many.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.3 Fisher's rate of two two-year projects
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q3
- concept_id: u3-fisher-rate-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 100*((-50000+sqrt(50000**2+4*100000*160000))/(2*100000)-1)

Project A requires 300,000 € and generates 100,000 € and 260,000 € in years 1 and 2; project B requires 200,000 € and generates 150,000 € and 100,000 €. Their Fisher's rate is:

a) 3.94%
b) 11.24%
c) 53.94%
d) 17.54%

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Equating the NPVs with $x = 1 + r$: $-300{,}000 + 100{,}000/x + 260{,}000/x^2 = -200{,}000 + 150{,}000/x + 100{,}000/x^2$. Multiplying by $x^2$ and grouping gives $100{,}000x^2 + 50{,}000x - 160{,}000 = 0$, so $x = \left(-50{,}000 + \sqrt{50{,}000^2 + 4 \times 100{,}000 \times 160{,}000}\right)/200{,}000 = (-50{,}000 + 257{,}875.94)/200{,}000 = 1.0394$, a Fisher's rate of 3.94% (both NPVs are then 36,882.86 €).

- b) This is the IRR of project A ($300{,}000x^2 - 100{,}000x - 260{,}000 = 0$), where its own NPV is zero, not the rate where the two NPVs are equal.
- c) The sign of the $x$ term was lost when grouping, $100{,}000x^2 - 50{,}000x - 160{,}000 = 0$, which gives $x = 1.5394$.
- d) This is the IRR of project B ($200{,}000x^2 - 150{,}000x - 100{,}000 = 0$), a property of one project, not of the pair.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.4 Capital cost from the balance sheet
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q4
- concept_id: u3-wacc-from-balance-sheet
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 100*((6+4.8)/18*0.14+7.2/18*0.06)

A company is financed with capital of 6,000,000 €, reserves of 4,800,000 € and debt of 7,200,000 €. The cost of its equity is estimated at 14% and the average cost of its debt at 6%. Its capital cost $K_{WACC}$ is:

a) 8.67%
b) 10.00%
c) 10.80%
d) 9.20%

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Equity is capital plus reserves, $6{,}000{,}000 + 4{,}800{,}000 = 10{,}800{,}000$ €, that is $10.8/18 = 60\%$ of the 18,000,000 € of funds, and debt is 40%. Then $K_{WACC} = 0.60 \times 14\% + 0.40 \times 6\% = 8.40\% + 2.40\% = 10.80\%$.

- a) The reserves were left out of equity, so equity weighed $6/18$ and debt $12/18$; reserves are retained profit and belong to equity.
- b) This is the simple average $(14\% + 6\%)/2$; the costs were not weighted by the financial structure.
- d) The weights were swapped, $0.40 \times 14\% + 0.60 \times 6\%$, giving equity the weight of the debt.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.5 The largest outlay worth paying
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q5
- concept_id: u3-max-outlay-npv
- format: identify
- asks: definition

A company discounts at a rate $k$ and is offered a project with known flows over a few years and an outlay still to be negotiated. The maximum outlay for which the project is interesting (NPV ≥ 0) is:

a) The present value of its future cash flows discounted at $k$
b) The sum of its future cash flows, without discounting
c) The present value of its future cash flows discounted at its IRR
d) Its year 1 cash flow divided by $k$, as if that flow were a perpetuity

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Writing the outlay as an unknown $X$, $NPV = -X + \sum_t Q_t/(1+k)^t \geq 0$ holds while $X$ does not exceed the present value of the flows at $k$; this is how the key of the examples finds $X \leq 706{,}447.19$ for project B at 8%.

- b) The undiscounted sum is the limit only at a rate of 0%; at any positive $k$ it overstates what the project is worth today.
- c) The IRR depends on the outlay that is still unknown, so it cannot fix it; and the decision is taken at the company's rate $k$, not at the IRR.
- d) The flows last a finite number of years; dividing one flow by $k$ values an endless stream that the project does not provide.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.6 Same outlay, same total, different timing
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q6
- concept_id: u3-timing-of-flows
- format: cause-effect
- asks: comparison

Projects A and B both require 100,000 €. A generates 90,000 €, 40,000 € and 20,000 € in years 1 to 3; B generates 20,000 €, 40,000 € and 90,000 €. At a discount rate of 8%:

a) Both have the same NPV, because their undiscounted flows add up to the same total
b) A has the higher NPV, because its largest flow is discounted over fewer years
c) B has the higher NPV, because its largest flow arrives at the end
d) They cannot be compared by NPV, only by the payback period

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
The factor $(1+k)^t$ grows with the year, so a large flow received early loses less value. At 8%, $NPV_A = 33{,}503.53$ € and $NPV_B = 24{,}256.97$ €: A is ahead although both totals are 150,000 €.

- a) The totals are equal only before discounting; at 8% each flow is divided by a different factor, so the NPVs differ.
- c) Receiving the largest flow later lowers its present value, it does not raise it: this inverts the effect of discounting.
- d) The NPV compares any two projects at a given rate; the payback ignores discounting and is the weaker tool here.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.7 Payback with a negative year 1
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q7
- concept_id: u3-payback-negative-flow
- format: what-happens
- asks: application

A project requires 1,200 and generates −200, 300, 500, 200, 400 and 400 in years 1 to 6. Under the payback criterion:

a) It cannot be assessed, because one of its flows after year 0 is negative
b) The negative flow is ignored and the outlay is recovered in year 4
c) The negative flow is added to the outlay and the outlay is never recovered
d) Its cumulative flows must first offset the year 1 deficit, and the outlay is recovered at the end of year 5

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
The cumulative flows are −200, 100, 600, 800 and 1,200, so the 1,200 is recovered exactly at the end of year 5, the payback of project X in the key of Exercise 3.

- a) A negative flow does not stop the method; it only delays the recovery, and the key computes a payback of 5 years.
- b) Dropping the −200 gives cumulative flows 300, 800, 1,000, 1,400 and a recovery during year 4, which overstates how fast the money comes back.
- c) Adding the −200 to the outlay is correct (1,400 to recover), but the later flows add up to 1,800, so the recovery still happens, at the end of year 5.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q8
- concept_id: u3-exclusive-vs-independent
- format: identify
- asks: comparison

Three projects have IRRs of 14% (A), 11% (B) and 9% (C), and the cost of capital is 10%. The NPV profiles of A and B cross at a Fisher's rate of 12%, with B having the larger NPV at 0%. Which projects does the company undertake if they are independent, and which if they are mutually exclusive?

a) Independent: A only; mutually exclusive: A
b) Independent: A, B and C; mutually exclusive: A
c) Independent: A and B; mutually exclusive: B
d) Independent: A and B; mutually exclusive: A

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
Independent projects are accepted whenever their IRR exceeds 10% (positive NPV): A and B, not C. If only one can be accepted, the choice is the higher NPV at 10%; since 10% is below the Fisher's rate of 12% and B leads at 0%, B's profile is still above A's at 10%, so B is chosen.

- a) B also has an IRR above the 10% cost of capital, so as an independent project it is accepted too.
- b) C has an IRR of 9%, below 10%, so its NPV is negative and it is rejected even if independent.
- d) Choosing A follows the IRR ranking, which holds only above the 12% Fisher's rate; at 10% B has the higher NPV.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x: Examples PDF, Exercises 5 and 6 (mutually exclusive projects, Fisher's rates); 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercises 7 and 8.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.9 Decision intervals of two projects
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q9
- concept_id: u3-no-project-rate
- format: identify
- asks: application

Two mutually exclusive projects: P has an IRR of 9% and Q an IRR of 13%; P has the larger NPV at 0%, and their Fisher's rate is 4%. For which discount rates does the company choose Q, and above which rate does it choose no project?

a) Q for rates between 4% and 13%; no project above 13%
b) Q for rates below 4%; no project above 9%
c) Q for rates between 9% and 13%; no project above 13%
d) Q for rates between 4% and 9%; no project above 9%

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
P leads below the 4% crossing, Q leads above it; Q keeps a positive NPV up to its IRR of 13%, while P's NPV is already negative above 9%. Above 13% both NPVs are negative, so no project is chosen, as in the conclusions of Exercises 5 and 6 of the examples.

- b) Below 4% the project with the larger NPV at 0% leads, which is P, not Q; and Q still has a positive NPV between 9% and 13%.
- c) Q is already above P from the 4% crossing; it does not wait until P's NPV becomes negative at 9%.
- d) Above 9% only P becomes unacceptable; Q stays positive up to its own IRR of 13%, so it is still chosen there.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.h: B06.10 Why the two criteria disagree
chunks.x:
- id: B06-Q10
- concept_id: u3-conflict-cause
- format: cause-effect
- asks: cause

At the company's rate of 5%, project A (IRR 15%) has a lower NPV than project B (IRR 11%), although both are acceptable. The reason is that:

a) One of the IRRs must be wrong, because NPV and IRR always rank projects alike
b) The discount rate lies below the Fisher's rate of the pair, where B's profile is still above A's
c) A's IRR exceeds the discount rate by more, so A's NPV must be negative
d) The NPV ignores the flows received after the outlay is recovered

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
The IRR ranking describes the profiles where they cut the horizontal axis; the NPV ranking at 5% describes them at 5%. If the profiles cross at a Fisher's rate above 5%, B is above A to the left of the crossing and A above B to the right, so the two criteria disagree at 5%, as in Exercise 9 of the sheet below its Fisher's rate of about 5%.

- a) The rankings can legitimately differ: they agree only on the side of the Fisher's rate where the higher-IRR project leads.
- c) An IRR above the discount rate means a positive NPV, not a negative one; both projects are acceptable at 5%.
- d) Ignoring the flows after the recovery is the limitation of the payback, not of the NPV, which counts every flow.

chunks.t: Two-year IRR, Fisher's rate and decision intervals
chunks.x:
3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 9 (b); Examples PDF, Exercise 5 (c).

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: Bank B07 — Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). Content: Topic 4 (The Production Function), Slides 6 to 43, and Exercise 1 of the examples PDF.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.1 Pairs of objectives that conflict
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q1
- concept_id: u4-objectives-contradictions
- format: false-statement
- asks: classification

The course names the pairs of objectives of the production function that can contradict each other. Which one of the following pairs is NOT among them:

a) Cost and quality
b) Flexibility and cost
c) Time of delivery and cost
d) Quality and flexibility

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
The four objectives are cost, quality, time of delivery and flexibility, and the slide on their contradictions names three pairs, every one of them against cost: cost - quality, flexibility - cost and time of delivery - cost (Topic 4, Slides 5 and 6). Quality and flexibility are not paired there.

- a) Cost and quality is named: better quality usually needs better materials and controls, which raise the cost.
- b) Flexibility and cost is named: many different products in small amounts lose the savings of standard production.
- c) Time of delivery and cost is named: delivering faster needs spare capacity or stocks, which cost money.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q2
- concept_id: u4-flexible-organization
- format: identify
- asks: classification

A workshop that makes custom interiors for business jets is organized as a flexible (intermittent) production system. Which of the following features belongs to its organization:

a) Job positions assigned by seniority, which bureaucratizes the company
b) Employee rotation and remuneration that depends on qualification
c) A narrow division of labour, so that each worker learns one simple task
d) Big volumes of standard products sold at a low price

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
Flexible production organizes the plant around teamwork, gives workers more responsibility, has fewer hierarchical levels, rotates its employees and pays according to qualification (Topic 4, Slide 15), which fits its complex, differentiated products and highly qualified workers (Slide 14).

- a) Assignment by seniority and bureaucratization describe the factory of rigid production, not of flexible production.
- c) A narrow division of labour with simple tasks is the job specialization of rigid production.
- d) Big volumes of standard products at a low price are the characteristics of rigid production.
