chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.3 Volume at which the rigid system becomes cheaper
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q3
- concept_id: u4-flexible-rigid-cost-crossover
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: (800000-200000)/(60-20)

A maker of drone propellers compares two production systems. The flexible one has fixed costs of 200,000 € a year and a variable cost of 60 € per unit; the rigid one has fixed costs of 800,000 € a year and a variable cost of 20 € per unit. Above what volume is the rigid system cheaper:

a) 10,000 units
b) 20,000 units
c) 15,000 units
d) 25,000 units

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
With $TC = FC + VC\,Q$ (Topic 4, Slide 37) the two total cost lines cross where $200{,}000 + 60\,Q = 800{,}000 + 20\,Q$, so $40\,Q = 600{,}000$ and $Q = 15{,}000$ units. Above that volume (zone B of Slide 17) the rigid system, with its lower variable cost, is cheaper; below it (zone A) the flexible one is.

- a) 10,000 units divides the difference of fixed costs by the flexible variable cost, 600,000/60, instead of by the difference of variable costs.
- b) 20,000 units divides only the rigid fixed costs by the difference of variable costs, 800,000/40, ignoring the flexible fixed costs.
- d) 25,000 units adds the two fixed costs, 1,000,000/40, instead of taking their difference.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.4 How a Gantt chart shows progress
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q4
- concept_id: u4-gantt-chart
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

A Gantt chart shows the current status of the schedule of a project by means of:

a) Arrows that link every activity with the activities that depend on it
b) Percent-complete shading of the bars and a vertical "TODAY" line
c) A network of nodes in which the longest path is marked
d) A table of the productivity of each production step

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
The Gantt chart is a bar chart with the scheduled start and stop dates of each step, and it shows the current schedule status with percent-complete shading and a vertical "TODAY" line (Topic 4, Slide 31).

- a) The course states that a Gantt chart normally does not show the dependency relationships between activities.
- c) A network of nodes with a longest path is a different planning tool, not the bar chart of Henry Gantt.
- d) Productivity indexes belong to the control of efficiency, measured a posteriori, not to the Gantt chart.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.5 Volume for a target profit
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q5
- concept_id: u4-target-profit-volume
- format: numeric
- asks: application
- calc: (90000+450000)/(120-75)

A supplier of aircraft seat belts has fixed costs of 450,000 € a year, sells each belt at 120 € and spends 75 € of variable cost per belt. How many belts must it sell to earn an operating profit of 90,000 €:

a) 12,000 belts
b) 10,000 belts
c) 2,000 belts
d) 4,500 belts

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
From $\text{Profit} = Q\,m - FC$ (Topic 4, Slides 37 and 39), $Q = (\text{Profit} + FC)/m$, with $m = 120 - 75 = 45$ €: $Q = (90{,}000 + 450{,}000)/45 = 540{,}000/45 = 12{,}000$ belts, the same step as part (b) of Examples PDF, Exercise 1.

- b) 10,000 belts is the break-even point, 450,000/45: it gives zero profit, not 90,000 €.
- c) 2,000 belts covers only the target profit, 90,000/45, and forgets that the fixed costs must be paid first.
- d) 4,500 belts divides profit plus fixed costs by the price, 540,000/120, instead of by the unit margin.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.6 Operating leverage from the cost data
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q6
- concept_id: u4-ol-calculation
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 50000*(40-25)/(50000*(40-25)-500000)

A maker of cockpit display brackets sells 50,000 units a year at 40 € each, with a variable cost of 25 € per unit and fixed costs of 500,000 € a year. Its operating leverage is:

a) 1.5
b) 2.0
c) 0.33
d) 3.0

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
$Q\,m = 50{,}000 \times (40 - 25) = 750{,}000$ € and the operating profit is $750{,}000 - 500{,}000 = 250{,}000$ €, so $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC) = 750{,}000/250{,}000 = 3$ (Topic 4, Slide 40). The same value follows from $Q^* = 500{,}000/15 = 33{,}333$ units and $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ (Slide 42).

- a) 1.5 divides the total margin by the fixed costs, 750,000/500,000, instead of by the operating profit.
- b) 2.0 divides the fixed costs by the operating profit, 500,000/250,000, which leaves out the margin of the units.
- c) 0.33 is profit over total margin, 250,000/750,000, the inverse of the operating leverage.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.7 Margin of safety in percentage
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q7
- concept_id: u4-margin-of-safety
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: (18000-360000/(90-60))/(360000/(90-60))*100

A maker of satellite antenna mounts has fixed costs of 360,000 € a year, a price of 90 € and a variable cost of 60 € per mount, and it sells 18,000 mounts. Its margin of safety in percentage, as defined by the course, is:

a) 33.3%
b) 66.7%
c) 50.0%
d) 150.0%

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
The break-even point is $Q^* = 360{,}000/(90 - 60) = 12{,}000$ mounts, and the course's percentage margin of safety is $MS = (Q - Q^*)/Q^* = (18{,}000 - 12{,}000)/12{,}000 = 50\%$ (Topic 4, Slides 37 and 43): sales are 50% above the break-even volume.

- a) 33.3% divides the 6,000 mounts above the break-even point by the actual volume, 18,000, instead of by the break-even volume of the slide.
- b) 66.7% is $Q^*/Q$, the share of sales needed to break even, not the distance above it.
- d) 150.0% is $Q/Q^*$, which forgets to subtract the break-even volume first.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.8 Role of Jidoka and Poka Yoke
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q8
- concept_id: u4-just-in-time
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: classification

In a Just in Time production system, Jidoka and Poka Yoke are:

a) Mechanisms to support quality
b) Mechanisms of visual control
c) The tools of internal organization
d) The forms of plant distribution

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
The course lists the elements of Just in Time with their tools: job cells for internal organization, the U shape for plant distribution, Jidoka and Poka Yoke as mechanisms to support quality, and Andon, control panels, work sheets and Kanban as mechanisms of visual control (Topic 4, Slides 20 and 21).

- b) The visual control mechanisms are Andon, control panels, work sheets and Kanban, not Jidoka and Poka Yoke.
- c) The internal organization of Just in Time is based on job cells, a different element of the system.
- d) The plant distribution of Just in Time is the U shape, not a quality mechanism.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.h: B07.9 From a functional to a product layout
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q9
- concept_id: u4-layout-comparison
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

An engine overhaul shop that grouped similar machines by function reorganizes its plant into a product layout, with one line that follows the sequence of operations. Which change should it expect:

a) A higher use of each machine and easier replacement of machines
b) More handling wastes when the materials are transported
c) Easier incentive programmes defined for each employee
d) Less work in process and simpler planning, but a less flexible plant

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
The product layout has little work in process, less space for transport and storage, simpler planning and control and a flow of materials that is easy to anticipate, but it is inflexible, depends on the slowest machine and needs a high investment (Topic 4, Slide 25).

- a) A high use of the machines and easy replacement of machines are advantages of the functional layout the shop is leaving.
- b) Handling wastes in transport are a disadvantage of the functional layout; the product layout reduces transport.
- c) Incentive programmes per employee are difficult to define in a product layout; a specific incentive system per worker is an advantage of the functional layout.

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
- id: B07-Q10
- concept_id: u4-planning-vs-control
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

In the course, production control is:

a) The effort to ensure that the production plans or schedules are met
b) The determination of what products to produce and where, when and how to produce them
c) The measurement of the productivity of the factors after production
d) The dispatching of notices to the operators so that they begin work

chunks.t: Objectives, layouts, planning and cost analysis
chunks.x:
Production planning decides what to produce and where, when and how; production control is the effort to ensure that those plans or schedules are met (Topic 4, Slide 27).

- b) Deciding what, where, when and how to produce is the definition of production planning, not of control.
- c) Measuring productivity a posteriori is the control of efficiency of Part IV, not the definition of production control.
- d) Dispatching notices to the operators is only the fifth step of the planning and control process, not its definition.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: Bank B08 — Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong). The examples PDF has no multiple-choice part: this is a practice format of the portal. Content: Topic 5, Slides 14, 17, 25-28 and 36-37; topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-3; PED Exercises SOL.pdf, Exercises 2-3.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.1 Income after a price rise with elastic demand
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q1
- concept_id: u5-revenue-after-price-rise
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 8000 * (1 - 1.5 * 0.08) * 250 * 1.08

Flight-data recorders currently bring their maker an income of 2,000,000 m.u. a year (8,000 recorders at 250 m.u.). Management plans an 8% price increase, knowing that buyers react with an elasticity of 1.5 in absolute value. Measuring every change against the current figures, what income should the maker expect after the increase:

a) $2{,}160{,}000$ m.u.
b) $1{,}900{,}800$ m.u.
c) $1{,}760{,}000$ m.u.
d) $2{,}419{,}200$ m.u.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
With the sign of the law of demand, $\%\Delta Q = (-1.5) \times 8\% = -12\%$, so the quantity falls to $8{,}000 \times 0.88 = 7{,}040$ units while the price rises to $250 \times 1.08 = 270$ m.u. Income is $I = P \cdot Q = 270 \times 7{,}040 = 1{,}900{,}800$ m.u., below the initial $2{,}000{,}000$ m.u.: with elastic demand a price rise lowers income.

- a) 2,160,000 m.u. sells the initial 8,000 units at the new price, ignoring the reaction of the quantity demanded.
- c) 1,760,000 m.u. multiplies the new quantity of 7,040 units by the old price of 250 m.u. instead of the new one.
- d) 2,419,200 m.u. raises the quantity by 12% instead of lowering it: the negative sign of the elasticity has been ignored.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.2 Point elasticity on a linear demand
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q2
- concept_id: u5-point-elasticity-linear
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: -30 * 200 / (18000 - 30 * 200)

The yearly demand for an inspection-drone software licence is $Q_d = 18{,}000 - 30\,p$, and the current price is $p = 200$ m.u. The point price elasticity of demand at this price, computed as in Exercise 3 of the course's elasticity sheet, is:

a) −2.00
b) −0.33
c) −1,800
d) −0.50

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
At $p = 200$ m.u. the quantity is $q = 18{,}000 - 30 \times 200 = 12{,}000$ licences, and the derivative of the demand is $dq/dp = -30$. Then $E_d = (dq/dp)\,(p/q) = -30 \times 200/12{,}000 = -0.50$: the demand is inelastic at this price.

- a) −2.00 is the inverse of the right value, the ratio $q/p$ divided by the slope: the fraction has been turned upside down.
- b) −0.33 divides by the intercept 18,000 instead of by the quantity actually demanded at 200 m.u.
- c) −1,800 multiplies the slope by $q/p$ instead of $p/q$, which gives a number with units, not a dimensionless elasticity.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q3
- concept_id: u5-revenue-observed-change
- format: numeric
- asks: application
- calc: 108 * 6000

A pilot-training school cuts the price of its simulator hour from 120 m.u. to 108 m.u., and the hours sold each month rise from 5,000 to 6,000. Its new monthly income from simulator hours is:

a) $648{,}000$ m.u.
b) $540{,}000$ m.u.
c) $720{,}000$ m.u.
d) $594{,}000$ m.u.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Income is $I = P \cdot Q = 108 \times 6{,}000 = 648{,}000$ m.u., up from $120 \times 5{,}000 = 600{,}000$ m.u. It agrees with the elasticity: with the initial values as the base, $\%\Delta Q = +20\%$ and $\%\Delta P = -10\%$, so $E_d = -2$, an elastic demand, for which a price cut raises income.

- b) 540,000 m.u. keeps the old 5,000 hours at the new price, as if the quantity did not respond to the price cut.
- c) 720,000 m.u. values the new 6,000 hours at the old price of 120 m.u. instead of the new 108 m.u.
- d) 594,000 m.u. lets the quantity rise only by 10%, the size of the price cut, as if the demand were unit elastic.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.4 Fifteen years of steady orders
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q4
- concept_id: u5-plc-stage-identification
- format: identify
- asks: application

A regional turboprop has been on the market for fifteen years. Its yearly orders stopped growing some years ago and now stay at a high, fairly stable level, with no sign yet of obsolescence. In which stage of the product life cycle is it:

a) Introduction
b) Growth
c) Maturity
d) Decline

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Maturity is the stage after growth, when sales no longer take off but stay high; it is the longest part of the life cycle, which fits fifteen years on the market.

- a) Introduction is the launch of a new product, not a model that has been sold for fifteen years.
- b) Growth is the stage in which sales take off; here the orders have stopped growing.
- d) Decline is the stage of obsolescence, with falling sales, and the statement says there is no sign of it.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.5 A curve that rises and falls
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q5
- concept_id: u5-plc-curve-shapes
- format: identify
- asks: classification

On the three sales curves of Slide 26, one curve rises quickly and then falls soon after its peak. Which kind of product does it represent (reading of the figure):

a) A fashion product
b) An immediate failure
c) A product of a dilated life
d) A product still in its introduction stage

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Reading the curves of Slide 26: the curve that rises and then falls (B) is the fashion product; the curve whose sales grow and then stay (A) is the product of a dilated life, and the one that falls almost at once (C) is the immediate failure.

- b) An immediate failure falls almost at once, without the quick rise that this curve shows.
- c) A product of a dilated life keeps its sales after they grow instead of losing them soon after the peak.
- d) A curve that has already peaked and fallen is past introduction, the launching stage of the product.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q6
- concept_id: u5-pricing-objectives-approaches
- format: false-statement
- asks: classification

Which one of the following statements about the price decisions is FALSE:

a) The price influences the demand and reinforces the image of the product
b) Pricing objectives can be maximizing profit, maximizing sales or achieving a certain market share
c) Cost-plus pricing and break-even analysis are methods of the cost approach
d) In the demand approach the price is set by adding a mark-up to the cost of the good

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Adding a mark-up to the cost of the good is cost-plus pricing, a method of the cost approach. The course names three approaches (competition, demand and cost), and only the cost approach starts from the cost of the good.

- a) Slide 27 gives these two reasons why the price matters, so the statement is true.
- b) Slide 27 lists exactly these pricing objectives, aligned with the marketing objectives, so it is true.
- c) Slide 28 places both methods under the cost approach, so the statement is true.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q7
- concept_id: u5-intermediary-functions
- format: true-statement
- asks: definition

Which one of the following is a function of the intermediaries of a distribution channel, according to the course:

a) Manufacturing the goods they distribute, so that the producer can concentrate on marketing
b) Offering a wide product mix from different producers
c) Choosing the target segment and the positioning of the producer's product
d) Designing the brand name and the logo of the products they carry

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Slide 36 lists the functions of intermediaries: improving exchange efficiency, helping match supply and demand, offering a wide product mix from different producers, managing logistics, and other marketing functions such as financing, market information and storage.

- a) Intermediaries operate between the producer and the final buyer; production stays with the producer.
- c) Segmentation and positioning are strategies of the producer's strategic marketing, not tasks of the channel.
- d) Brand and logo are product attributes decided by the owner of the brand, not a function of distribution.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.8 Steps for selecting a channel
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q8
- concept_id: u5-channel-selection-order
- format: ordering
- asks: definition

In what order does the course list the steps for selecting a distribution channel:

a) Define the channel; set the distribution objectives; choose intensive, selective or exclusive distribution
b) Choose intensive, selective or exclusive distribution; define the channel; set the distribution objectives
c) Set the distribution objectives; choose intensive, selective or exclusive distribution; define the channel
d) Set the distribution objectives; define the channel; choose intensive, selective or exclusive distribution

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Slide 37 lists three steps: first the objectives of the distribution (buying habits, customer, product, company and competitors), then the distribution strategy (intensive, selective or exclusive), and finally the definition of the channel, with the characteristics of each intermediary and their coordination.

- a) The channel is defined last, once the objectives and the intensity are known, not at the start.
- b) The intensity is a strategy chosen to meet the objectives, so the objectives cannot come last.
- d) This swaps the last two steps: the intensity is chosen before the channel and its intermediaries are defined.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.9 A light aircraft for first licences
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q9
- concept_id: u5-positioning-bases
- format: identify
- asks: application

A maker of light aircraft presents its two-seater in every campaign as "the aircraft for flying clubs and students taking their first licence". On which basis is this positioning built:

a) The price-quality relationship
b) A comparison with another product
c) A geographical segmentation criterion
d) The characteristics of the user

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
The message defines the product by who uses it (flying clubs and students), which is positioning based on user characteristics, one of the bases listed on Slide 14.

- a) The message says nothing about price or quality, so it is not a price-quality positioning.
- b) No other aircraft is named or compared with the two-seater in the message.
- c) Geographical criteria divide a market into segments by area; they are not a basis for positioning.

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.h: B08.10 Elasticity with respect to advertising
chunks.x:
- id: B08-Q10
- concept_id: u5-elasticity-other-factor
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: application

A drone-services firm raises its advertising budget by 20%, and the demand for its services rises by 5%, all else equal. Using the elasticity of the demand of Slide 17, the demand with respect to advertising is:

a) Inelastic, since the elasticity is 0.25, below 1
b) Elastic, since the demand responds to the advertising budget
c) Unit elastic, since both changes have the same sign
d) Not measurable, since an elasticity is only defined with respect to the price

chunks.t: Revenue, life cycle, pricing and channels
chunks.x:
Slide 17 defines the elasticity of the demand with respect to any factor, mainly the marketing-mix variables: $E = 5\%/20\% = 0.25 < 1$, so the demand is inelastic, not very sensitive to the advertising budget.

- b) Any response gives a non-zero elasticity; the demand is elastic only when the ratio is above 1.
- c) Unit elasticity needs equal percentage changes (ratio 1), not merely changes of the same sign.
- d) Slide 17 applies the elasticity to any factor of the demand, not only to the price.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: Bank B09 — Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The multiple-choice part is a practice format of the portal: the examples PDF has none. Content: Topic 6, Slides 5, 7-10, 13-14, 16, 18 and 23.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.1 Sharing out the plant budget
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q1
- concept_id: u6-management-levels
- format: identify
- asks: classification

The manager of an aero-engine plant decides how next year's budget of the plant is shared out among its machining, assembly and test departments. Which management level and type of decision is this?

a) Top management, a strategic decision
b) Middle management, a tactical decision
c) Low management, an operational decision
d) Top management, a general decision

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
A plant manager sits between the top management of the company and the first-line supervisors of the shop floor, and distributing resources among the departments of one plant is a tactical decision: tactical decisions are taken by middle management.

- a) Strategic decisions concern the firm as a whole (markets, products, growth), not the internal budget of one plant.
- c) Operational decisions of first-line supervisors deal with the daily work of a team, such as shifts or task assignments, not a yearly budget for several departments.
- d) General decisions are those of top management covering the whole firm; this one is limited to one plant and its departments.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.2 A strike on the final assembly line
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q2
- concept_id: u6-mintzberg-roles
- format: identify
- asks: application

A sudden strike stops the final assembly line of a business-jet maker, and the plant director steps in at once to restore production. Which of Mintzberg's managerial roles is the director playing?

a) Liaison, an interpersonal role
b) Monitor, an informational role
c) Disturbance handler, a decisional role
d) Entrepreneur, a decisional role

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
Reacting to an unexpected crisis that disrupts the firm is the disturbance handler role, one of the four decisional roles. The slide lists the roles by name only; the meaning used here is the usual one of Mintzberg's classification.

- a) The liaison role builds contacts with people outside the manager's own unit; it is not about solving a crisis inside the plant.
- b) The monitor role gathers information about the firm and its environment; here the director acts on a problem rather than collecting data.
- d) The entrepreneur role starts planned changes and new projects on the manager's initiative, whereas a strike is an unplanned disturbance imposed from outside.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q3
- concept_id: u6-mintzberg-roles
- format: false-statement
- asks: classification

Which pairing of a managerial role with its group of Mintzberg's classification is false?

a) Liaison: interpersonal roles
b) Monitor: informational roles
c) Entrepreneur: decisional roles
d) Disseminator: decisional roles

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
The disseminator is an informational role, with the monitor and the spokesperson; the decisional roles are entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator.

- a) This pairing is true: the interpersonal roles are figurehead, leader and liaison.
- b) This pairing is true: the monitor is the first of the three informational roles.
- c) This pairing is true: the entrepreneur heads the list of the four decisional roles.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.4 A fuel that is suddenly banned
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q4
- concept_id: u6-decision-types
- format: identify
- asks: application

A small launch-services firm learns that the propellant its engines use will be banned within a year. The situation has no precedent in the firm, and there is no ready list of alternatives. Which type of decision must its managers take?

a) An innovative (not planned) decision
b) A routine (planned) decision
c) An adaptable decision
d) An operational decision

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
The problem is unusual and ambiguous and the alternatives are ambiguous and not planned, which defines the innovative decision.

- b) A routine decision needs a known, well-defined problem with known alternatives, the opposite of a situation with no precedent.
- c) An adaptable decision lies in between, for problems and alternatives that are partly known; here nothing is known in advance.
- d) Operational refers to the level of first-line supervisors, not to the type of problem and alternatives, and a threat to the firm's engines is far beyond daily work.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.5 From supervisor to general manager
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q5
- concept_id: u6-managerial-skills
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

An engineer who supervised a composite-layup team is promoted, years later, to general manager of the whole company. How does the mix of managerial skills the job demands change?

a) The technical skill weighs more and the conceptual skill less
b) The interpersonal skill stops being needed, because the manager no longer leads a team directly
c) The conceptual skill weighs more and the technical skill less, while the interpersonal skill remains necessary
d) The mix does not change, because the three skills weigh the same at every level

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
Moving up the hierarchy, the share of the conceptual skill (seeing the firm as a whole) grows and the share of the technical skill (understanding how things operate) falls; the interpersonal skill is needed at every level.

- a) This inverts the trend: technical skill weighs most in low management and conceptual skill in top management.
- b) Interacting with people at work successfully is needed at every level, including top management.
- d) The slide shows different proportions of the three skills along the hierarchy, so the mix does change with the level.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.6 The four steps of planning
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q6
- concept_id: u6-planning-steps
- format: ordering
- asks: definition

Which list gives the main steps of planning in the order of the course?

a) Defining strategic objectives, developing forecasts, deciding on a course of action, developing alternative courses of action
b) Developing forecasts, defining strategic objectives, developing alternative courses of action, deciding on a course of action
c) Establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations, taking corrective action if required
d) Recognizing the problem, gathering information, considering alternatives, analysing the alternatives

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
Planning starts from forecasts, sets the strategic objectives, develops the alternative courses of action that could reach them and finally decides on one of them.

- a) The objectives rest on the forecasts, so forecasting comes first, and a course of action cannot be chosen before the alternatives have been developed.
- c) These are the activities of controlling, the function that checks the results against the standards that planning has set.
- d) These are the first four steps of the decision-making process, not the steps of planning.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.7 Part of the structural configuration
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q7
- concept_id: u6-structural-configuration
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Among the factors that determine the organizational structure, which of the following is listed as an element of the structural configuration rather than as a factor of its own?

a) The span of control
b) Standardization
c) Centralization
d) Formalization

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
The structural configuration groups the type of departmentalization, the number of layers (hierarchical levels), the span of control and the size of the administrative component.

- b) Standardization is a factor of its own on the slide, next to specialization, formalization, centralization and the structural configuration.
- c) Centralization is a separate factor, which describes whether decision-making is centralized or decentralized.
- d) Formalization is listed as a separate factor, not inside the structural configuration.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.8 The quality office and the legal department
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q8
- concept_id: u6-parts-formal-structure
- format: identify
- asks: application

In a satellite factory, a quality-engineering office designs the inspection procedures that the integration technicians follow, while a legal department and a cafeteria serve the factory without taking part in the production flow. To which parts of the formal structure do the office and the legal department belong?

a) Middle line and operating core
b) Operating core and strategic apex
c) Support staff and technostructure
d) Technostructure and support staff

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
The analysts who design systems and processes form the technostructure, and the units outside the operating workflow form the support staff; the office designs procedures and the legal department lies outside the workflow.

- a) The middle line is middle management and the operating core is the technicians who integrate the satellites; neither designs procedures nor serves from outside the flow.
- b) The strategic apex is top management, and the operating core does the production work, which the legal department does not do.
- c) This swaps the two parts: the designers of procedures are the technostructure, and the unit outside the workflow is the support staff.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q9
- concept_id: u6-configuration-environment
- format: identify
- asks: comparison

A large, mature maker of standard aircraft fasteners works in a stable and simple environment; a large aerospace engineering consultancy works in a stable but complex one. Which basic configurations fit them, in that order?

a) Simple structure and division organization
b) Machine bureaucracy and professional bureaucracy
c) Professional bureaucracy and machine bureaucracy
d) Adhocracy and simple structure

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
The machine bureaucracy is the configuration of mature, big organizations in a stable and simple environment, and the professional bureaucracy that of big organizations in a stable but complex environment.

- a) The simple structure fits start-ups and very small businesses, and the division organization diversified businesses in more dynamic environments; neither matches a large, stable firm.
- c) This inverts the two: the stable but complex environment of qualified professionals is that of the professional bureaucracy, not of the fastener maker.
- d) The adhocracy is a complementary structure for specific projects and the simple structure is for very small firms, so neither suits a large, mature company.

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.h: B09.10 Rating pilots and linking their pay
chunks.x:
- id: B09-Q10
- concept_id: u6-hr-staffing
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Six months after hiring a group of pilots, the human resources department of an airline rates the performance of each one and links part of their pay to the rating. Which activities of human resources management are these?

a) Performance appraisal and compensation, both part of staffing
b) Recruitment and selection, both part of staffing
c) Motivation and leadership, both part of directing
d) Training and communication, both part of directing

chunks.t: Scenarios: levels, roles and structures
chunks.x:
Rating employees already in the firm is performance appraisal, and linking pay to it belongs to compensation and incentive programmes; both are listed under staffing.

- b) Recruitment and selection attract and choose candidates before they are hired, while these pilots are already employees.
- c) Motivation and leadership belong to directing and do not consist of rating performance or setting pay.
- d) Training belongs to staffing, not to directing, and neither training nor communication rates performance or sets pay.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: Bank B10 — Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten multiple-choice questions written for the bank (four options, one right answer; +0.25 right, −0.08 wrong, 0 blank). The examples PDF has no multiple-choice part and no Topic 7 exercise; content from Topic 7, Slides 11-19.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.1 A turbofan that burns less fuel
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q1
- concept_id: u7-product-vs-process
- format: identify
- asks: classification

An engine maker launches a new turbofan for regional jets that burns 15% less fuel than its previous model and sells it to airlines. On the product vs process pair, this is ...

a) a process innovation, because it lowers the operating costs of the airlines that use it
b) a product innovation, because the novelty is embodied in the output the firm sells
c) a process innovation, because any gain in efficiency is a process innovation
d) neither, because a 15% gain is too small to count as an innovation

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Product innovations are embodied in the outputs of an organization, its goods or services, like the hybrid car of Slide 11; the new turbofan is the engine maker's output.

- a) The airlines' lower costs are a benefit of using the new product; a process innovation changes the way the innovating firm itself produces or markets, which is not the case here.
- c) Process innovations often aim at efficiency of production, but a more efficient product sold to customers is still a product innovation; the pair depends on where the novelty lies.
- d) The size of the change decides between radical and incremental, a different pair; it does not stop the turbofan from being an innovation.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.2 Better solar cells on the same bus
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q2
- concept_id: u7-architectural-vs-component
- format: identify
- asks: application

A satellite manufacturer replaces the solar cells of its standard platform with cells of higher efficiency. The panels keep their size, mounting and electrical interface, and no other subsystem of the satellite changes. How does the course classify this change on the architectural vs component pair:

a) An architectural innovation, because a satellite is a system of subsystems
b) An architectural innovation, because more power changes the satellite's performance
c) Neither, because solar cells are bought from a supplier
d) A component innovation, because one component changes without significantly affecting the overall configuration

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Slide 13: a component (modular) innovation changes one or more components without significantly affecting the overall configuration of the system, which is what happens when only the cells change and every interface stays.

- a) Every satellite is a system; an architectural innovation needs a change in the overall design or in the way the components interact, and none happens here.
- b) Better performance does not make an innovation architectural; the classification depends on the configuration of the system, not on how much it improves.
- c) The classification is about what changes in the system, not about who makes the component; a supplied component can be the object of a component innovation.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.3 Electric motors for light aircraft
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q3
- concept_id: u7-competence-perspective
- format: identify
- asks: application

Electric propulsion for light training aircraft spreads. Firm E has built electric motors and battery packs for drones for twenty years; firm P has only ever built piston engines. On the competence pair, how should this innovation be classified:

a) Competence-enhancing for E and competence-destroying for P
b) Competence-destroying for both, because it is new to the light-aircraft market
c) Competence-enhancing for both, because both firms already build aircraft engines
d) It cannot be classified until the industry selects a dominant design

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Slide 12: the classification depends on whose perspective is taken. The innovation builds on E's existing knowledge base (competence-enhancing for E) and does not build on P's competencies, which it may render obsolete (competence-destroying for P).

- b) Novelty in a market is not the criterion; for E the innovation builds on existing knowledge, so it is not competence-destroying for every firm.
- c) P's knowledge is about piston engines, which electric propulsion does not build on; making propulsion units is not the same knowledge base.
- d) The competence pair is judged from each firm's knowledge base; it does not depend on the later selection of a dominant design (Slide 17).

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.4 Small gains from the first efforts
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q4
- concept_id: u7-s-curve-shape
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

A start-up has just begun developing a new battery chemistry for electric aircraft, and its first efforts bring only small gains in energy density. If it keeps investing effort, what does the course's S-curve of technology performance lead us to expect:

a) The gains will stay small for ever, because a slow start shows that the technology has no future
b) The gains will be the same for every additional unit of effort
c) The gains will speed up for a while and then slow down as the technology approaches its limit
d) The gains will be largest at the end, when the technology reaches its limit

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Plotted against effort, performance improves slowly at first, then quickly, and finally flattens as it approaches the limit of the technology (Slide 14); the start-up is in the first, flat part of the curve.

- a) A slow start is the normal first part of the S-curve, not a sign that the curve will never rise.
- b) Equal gains for every unit of effort would be a straight line, not the S-shape of the course.
- d) Near the limit the curve is flat, so the gains there are the smallest, not the largest.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q5
- concept_id: u7-discontinuous-technology
- format: identify
- asks: application

Which of the following is a discontinuous technology in the sense of the course:

a) A chemical thruster with a 5% higher specific impulse, developed from the firm's previous model
b) Electric (plasma) thrusters that keep a satellite in its orbit, a need until now met by chemical thrusters, built on an entirely different body of knowledge
c) A new satellite service for a market need that no earlier technology served
d) A chemical thruster that a regulator imposes as the industry standard

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
A discontinuous technology fulfils a similar market need by building on an entirely new knowledge base (Slide 15); station-keeping is the same need, and plasma propulsion rests on knowledge different from combustion.

- a) An improvement developed from the previous model builds on the same knowledge base; it moves along the existing S-curve instead of starting a new one.
- c) The definition requires a similar market need to an existing technology; a need that nothing served before does not fit it.
- d) Imposing a design as a standard says nothing about its knowledge base; besides, a dominant design is a de facto standard that need not be officially enforced (Slide 17).

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.6 Cumulative adopters after the early majority
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q6
- concept_id: u7-adopter-cumulative-shares
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 2.5 + 13.5 + 34

On the course's diffusion curve, what cumulative share of the population has adopted a technology once the whole early majority has adopted it:

a) 50%
b) 34%
c) 84%
d) 16%

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
The cumulative share adds the innovators (2.5%), the early adopters (13.5%) and the early majority (34%): $2.5 + 13.5 + 34 = 50$, so 50% (Slide 16, panel (a)).

- b) 34% is the share of the early majority alone, read from the bell curve, not the cumulative share.
- c) 84% is the cumulative share once the late majority has also adopted; it adds another 34%.
- d) 16% is the cumulative share at the end of the early adopters (2.5% + 13.5%), before any of the early majority.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.7 Early adopters among flight schools
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q7
- concept_id: u7-adopter-categories
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 0.135 * 600

A new electric trainer aircraft is expected to be adopted, in time, by all 600 flight schools of a region, following the adopter categories of the course. How many of these flight schools are early adopters:

a) 96 flight schools
b) 15 flight schools
c) 81 flight schools
d) 204 flight schools

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Early adopters are 13.5% of the adopters (Slide 16): $0.135 \times 600 = 81$ flight schools.

- a) 96 is 16% of 600, the cumulative share of innovators and early adopters together (or the share of the laggards), not the early adopters alone.
- b) 15 is 2.5% of 600, the innovators, who adopt before the early adopters.
- d) 204 is 34% of 600, the size of the early majority or of the late majority.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q8
- concept_id: u7-radical-vs-incremental
- format: identify
- asks: application

An airliner manufacturer considers four projects. Which one is a radical innovation in the sense of the course:

a) Retrofitting winglets to the wings of its current airliner
b) A software update that raises the take-off thrust of its current engines by 3%
c) A cabin with slightly wider seats in the same fuselage
d) A blended-wing-body airliner that merges wing and fuselage into a single lifting body, unlike any earlier tube-and-wing design

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
A radical innovation is very new and different from prior solutions (Slide 12); a blended wing body departs from the tube-and-wing solution of every earlier airliner.

- a) Winglets are a relatively minor change to the existing wing, an incremental innovation.
- b) A 3% thrust gain from a software update is a minor adjustment to existing practice, so it is incremental.
- c) Slightly wider seats in the same fuselage are a small adjustment to the existing cabin, an incremental change.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q9
- concept_id: u7-network-externalities
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: classification

A flight-planning platform becomes more valuable to each airline as more airlines use it, because route data and procedures are shared among its users. In the course's terms, the number of airlines using the platform is its ...

a) installed base
b) complementary goods
c) absorptive capacity
d) technological spillover

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
The installed base is the number of users of a particular good (Slide 19); through network externalities, the value of the platform to each user grows with that number.

- b) Complementary goods are additional goods and services that enhance the value of a good, such as applications for the platform, not the count of its users.
- c) Absorptive capacity is an organization's ability to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge (Slide 18), a capability of one firm.
- d) A technological spillover is the spread of R&D knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries (Slide 9), not a number of users.

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.h: B10.10 After the design is chosen
chunks.x:
- id: B10-Q10
- concept_id: u7-dominant-design-consequence
- format: what-happens
- asks: effect

Once an industry has selected a dominant design, what does the course say producers and customers do:

a) They keep developing and comparing several alternative designs with the same effort as before
b) They wait until a regulator officially enforces the design before investing in it
c) They focus on improving their efficiency in manufacturing, delivering, marketing or deploying that design
d) They abandon the design as soon as it reaches 50% of the market

chunks.t: Classifying aerospace innovations and reading adoption curves
chunks.x:
Slide 17: once the dominant design is selected, producers and customers focus their efforts on improving their efficiency in manufacturing, delivering, marketing or deploying it, rather than continuing to develop and consider alternative designs.

- a) This is the opposite of what the course says: after the selection the effort shifts away from alternative designs.
- b) A dominant design is a de facto standard: it may not be officially enforced or acknowledged, so nobody waits for a regulator.
- d) Holding usually 50% or more of the market is what makes a design dominant, not a reason to abandon it.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: Bank F01 — Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, 0 blank; the reasoning is required). Sources: 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf and 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercises 3 to 9; Examples PDF, Exercises 5 and 6; Topic 3, Slide 37. The Topic 3 deck has no investment-selection slides, so the criteria are those used in the problem sheet and its key.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.1 What the NPV adds up
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S1
- concept_id: u3-npv-definition

The NPV of a project is the sum of its net cash flows minus the initial outlay, with every flow counted at its nominal value whatever the year in which it arrives.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: That sum is only the NPV at a discount rate of 0%. The NPV discounts each flow to year 0, $NPV = -A + \sum_t Q_t/(1+k)^t$, so a flow received later is worth less today.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.2 The rate that cancels the NPV
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S2
- concept_id: u3-irr-definition

The internal rate of return of a project is the discount rate at which its NPV is equal to zero.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: This is the definition used in the key: the IRR is the rate that makes the NPV equal to 0, which is why a known IRR lets one solve for the initial outlay.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.3 Ranking two projects below the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S3
- concept_id: u3-irr-below-cost-of-capital

Two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 9% and 7%, and the cost of capital is 9.5%. Under the IRR criterion the company should undertake the project with the 9% IRR, because it ranks first.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: Ranking is not enough: a project is accepted only if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital. Both IRRs are below 9.5%, so both NPVs at 9.5% are negative and neither project is accepted.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.4 IRR above the discount rate
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S4
- concept_id: u3-irr-npv-relation

A project with conventional cash flows (an outlay followed by positive flows) has an IRR of 10%. If it is valued at a discount rate of 7%, its NPV is positive.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: The NPV of such a project falls as the rate rises and is zero at the IRR. At 7%, below the 10% IRR, it is therefore positive (IRR > k).

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S5
- concept_id: u3-payback-limits

The payback period takes into account every cash flow of the project, including those received after the initial outlay has been recovered.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: The payback is the time it takes to recover the initial investment, so it stops counting at that moment and ignores every later flow. Two projects with the same payback can differ greatly in what they return afterwards.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.6 Fisher's rate of one project
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S6
- concept_id: u3-fisher-rate-definition

Fisher's rate of a project is the discount rate at which the NPV of that project becomes zero.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: That is the IRR. Fisher's rate belongs to a pair of projects: it is the discount rate at which the two NPVs are equal, and it marks where the preferred project changes.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.7 The weighted average cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S7
- concept_id: u3-wacc-definition

The capital cost of a company is the average of the cost of its equity and the cost of its liabilities, each weighted by its share in the financial structure.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: Topic 3 defines $K_{WACC} = K_{EQ}\,E/(E+L) + K_L\,L/(E+L)$; the key of Exercise 8 uses this weighted cost as the cut-off rate for the IRR.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S8
- concept_id: u3-cost-of-equity

Equity has no cost for the company, because the company does not pay interest on the funds contributed by its owners.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: Every financial resource has a cost: liabilities have an explicit cost and equity an implicit (opportunity) cost, which enters the weighted average cost of capital.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S9
- concept_id: u3-npv-rate-sensitivity

For a project made of an initial outlay followed by positive cash flows, a higher discount rate gives a lower NPV.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: Each positive flow is divided by $(1+k)^t$, which grows with $k$, while the outlay at year 0 is not discounted; the NPV therefore decreases as the rate rises.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.h: F01.10 Equal NPVs at a zero rate
chunks.x:
- id: F01-S10
- concept_id: u3-fisher-rate-zero

If two projects have the same NPV at a discount rate of 0% (the same sum of net cash flows minus the outlay), then 0% is a Fisher's rate of that pair.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x: Fisher's rate is the rate at which both NPVs are equal; at 0% both NPVs equal their undiscounted sums, which are the same, so $r = 0\%$ solves the equation.

chunks.t: Investment selection criteria and the cost of capital
chunks.x:
Examples PDF, Exercise 5 (c), pair A–B ($x = 1$, FR = 0%), and Exercise 6 (c).

**Back to:** Problem Set - Business Management Problem Bank

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: Bank F02 — Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, 0 blank; every answer needs its reasoning). Content: Topic 4 (The Production Function), Slides 6 to 43.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.1 What a Gantt chart shows
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S1
- concept_id: u4-gantt-chart

A Gantt chart is a bar chart that normally shows the dependency relationships between the activities of a project, which makes it the preferred tool for planning complex projects.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: The Gantt chart shows the scheduled start and stop dates of each step, but it normally does not show the dependency relationships between activities and it is used for non-complex projects.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S2
- concept_id: u4-objectives-contradictions

Flexibility and cost are two objectives of the production function that can contradict each other.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: The four objectives (cost, quality, time of delivery and flexibility) can conflict, and flexibility - cost is one of the pairs named by the course: making many different products in small amounts loses the savings of standard, large-scale production.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S3
- concept_id: u4-rigid-production

Rigid (continuous) production is characterized by flexible volumes of production, highly qualified workers and equipment for general use.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: Those are the characteristics of flexible or intermittent production. Rigid production has big volumes, standard products sold at a low price and is capital intensive.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.4 Flexible versus rigid below the crossing volume
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S4
- concept_id: u4-flexible-rigid-cost-crossover

Below the volume at which the total cost lines of the two systems cross, a flexible production system is cheaper than a rigid one, because the rigid system starts with higher fixed costs.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: The rigid system's total cost starts higher (more fixed cost) and grows more slowly (less variable cost per unit), so at low volumes (zone A) the flexible system is cheaper and at high volumes (zone B) the rigid one is.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.5 Bottlenecks in a product layout
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S5
- concept_id: u4-product-layout

In a product layout the pace of the line is set by the slowest machine, and a problem in one machine affects the whole process.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: Both are disadvantages of the product layout listed by the course: time is set by the slowest machine (bottlenecks must be avoided) and a failure of one machine stops the whole flow.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.6 Inventories under Just in Time
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S6
- concept_id: u4-just-in-time

Just in Time production relies on large safety inventories of finished products so that every customer request can be served at once.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: Just in Time is based on requests and eliminates inventories; production is pulled by the orders, not served from stock.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S7
- concept_id: u4-partial-productivity

Labour productivity is a total productivity index, because labour is the main factor of production of most firms.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: Labour productivity (goods and services divided by labour) relates the output to one factor only, so it is a partial productivity index; the total index divides by labour, capital, raw materials and energy together.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.8 A higher price and the break-even point
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S8
- concept_id: u4-bep-unit-margin

If the selling price rises while the fixed costs and the variable cost per unit stay the same, the break-even point falls.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: $Q_0 = FC/(P - VC)$: a higher price raises the unit margin $m = P - VC$, and the same fixed costs are covered with fewer units.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.9 Sensitivity just above the break-even point
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S9
- concept_id: u4-operating-leverage-meaning

A firm that sells slightly more than its break-even volume sees its operating profit change by much more than 1% when its sales change by 1%.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$: when $Q$ is just above $Q^*$ the denominator is small, so the operating leverage is large and the effect on profit is more than proportional.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.h: F02.10 Margin of safety in monetary units
chunks.x:
- id: F02-S10
- concept_id: u4-margin-of-safety

The margin of safety in monetary units is the difference between the actual volume and the break-even volume multiplied by the selling price.

chunks.t: Production systems, costs and operating leverage
chunks.x: In monetary units the margin of safety is $(Q - Q^*)\,m$: the units above the break-even point multiplied by the unit margin, not by the price, because each extra unit adds only its margin to the profit.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: Bank F03 — Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, a short reason for each answer). Content: Topic 5, Slides 5-8, 12, 19, 24 and 35; topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-5; Examples PDF, Exercise 2.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.1 Where segmentation, positioning and price belong
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S1
- concept_id: u5-strategic-vs-operative

Market segmentation and the positioning of the product are formulated within strategic marketing, whereas setting the price of the product is a decision of operative marketing.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: Segmentation and positioning are the strategies formulated in the last phase of strategic marketing (the analysis system), while price is one of the 4 Ps that operative marketing (the action system) combines in the marketing mix.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S2
- concept_id: u5-sale-vs-marketing

Marketing differs from the sale in that marketing is a one-way process in which the company places its goods and services in front of the customer.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: The one-way process is the sale. Marketing is a two-way process: goods and services go to the customer, and information about what the customer wants comes back to the company.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.3 A new version inside an existing line
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S3
- concept_id: u5-range-extension-vs-depth

When an avionics firm adds a new model to one of its existing product lines, the extension (width) of its product range increases.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: The extension, or width (breadth), of the range is the number of product lines, which does not change. A new model inside an existing line increases the depth of that line (products per line) and the length of the range (total number of products).

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.4 Raising the price of a product with inelastic demand
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S4
- concept_id: u5-elasticity-income

If the demand for a product is inelastic, a rise in its price increases the income of the firm that sells it.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: With $\lvert E_d \rvert < 1$ a 1% price rise lowers the quantity demanded by less than 1%, so almost the same quantity is sold at a higher price and income $I = P \cdot Q$ rises.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.5 Several segments, several marketing mixes
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S5
- concept_id: u5-segmentation-strategies

A firm that targets two or more segments and develops a distinct product and a separate marketing mix for each of them follows a differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: That is the wide differentiated (multisegment) strategy. The differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy aims the product and the marketing message at a single, well-defined segment.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.6 Who the wholesaler sells to
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S6
- concept_id: u5-wholesaler

A wholesaler is an intermediary that sells to other intermediaries or to organisational buyers, but not to final consumers.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: This is the course's definition of the wholesaler; the intermediary that sells consumer goods to final consumers for their personal or household use is the retailer.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.7 The sign of the price elasticity coefficient
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S7
- concept_id: u5-elasticity-sign

By the law of demand the coefficient of price elasticity of demand is negative, which is why its absolute value is used to classify the demand as elastic or inelastic.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so the ratio of their percentage changes is negative; the course classifies the demand with $\lvert E_d \rvert$ compared with 1.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.8 Influencer campaigns and the product
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S8
- concept_id: u5-attributes-vs-communication

A campaign on social networks with technology influencers is one of the product attributes of a firm, because it builds the image of the product.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: The campaign belongs to the promotion (communication) policy of the marketing mix. The psychosocial attributes of the product are brand, design, packaging and quality, together with attributes such as warranty and post-sale service.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S9
- concept_id: u5-cross-elasticity

If the cross elasticity of demand between two goods is negative, the two goods are complementary.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: Cross elasticity is negative for complementary goods (a fall in the price of one raises the consumption of both) and positive for substitute goods.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.h: F03.10 How agents and brokers are paid
chunks.x:
- id: F03-S10
- concept_id: u5-agents-brokers

Merchandise agents and brokers take title to the products they distribute and earn their income from the margin between their buying and selling prices.

chunks.t: Marketing concepts, the marketing mix and elasticity
chunks.x: Agents and brokers bring buyers and sellers together without owning title to the products, and they are paid a commission for their services.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.h: Bank F04 — Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, 0 blank; a written reason for every answer). Content: Topic 6, Slides 3, 5-8, 14, 16, 20 and 23-24.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S1
- concept_id: u6-management-functions

Management is the process of setting and achieving goals through four basic functions, planning, organizing, leading and controlling, that use human, financial and material resources.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: This is the course's definition of management, and the four managerial functions are exactly planning, organizing, leading and controlling.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S2
- concept_id: u6-decision-types

An innovative decision is taken when the problem is known and well defined and the alternative solutions are planned in advance.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: A known, well-defined problem with known alternatives calls for a routine (planned) decision. An innovative (not planned) decision faces an unusual and ambiguous problem with ambiguous, unplanned alternatives.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.h: F04.3 Order of the decision-making process
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S3
- concept_id: u6-decision-process-order

In the decision-making process, the manager chooses an alternative first and only then analyses the alternatives that were considered.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: Analysing the alternatives is step 4 and choosing an alternative is step 5: the choice comes after the analysis, never before it.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.h: F04.4 Conceptual skills along the hierarchy
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S4
- concept_id: u6-managerial-skills

Conceptual skills, the ability to see the firm as a whole, weigh more in top management than in first-line supervision.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: The share of conceptual skills grows as one moves up the management hierarchy, while technical skills weigh most in low management; interpersonal skills are needed at every level.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S5
- concept_id: u6-recruitment-selection

When an avionics firm publishes a job offer on an engineering job board to attract applicants, it is carrying out the selection of personnel.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: Attracting applicants is recruitment, a Human Resources activity that comes before selection; selection is the later step that chooses among the candidates already recruited.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.h: F04.6 The key part of the division organization
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S6
- concept_id: u6-division-organization

In a division organization the middle line is the key part of the structure, and each autonomous division is itself organized as a bureaucracy.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: The divisions are autonomous, the middle line is the key part, top management coordinates their performance and outputs, and each division is a bureaucracy.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S7
- concept_id: u6-parts-formal-structure

The analysts who design the systems and processes of the firm belong to the technostructure, not to the support staff.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: The technostructure is formed by the analysts who design systems and processes; the support staff is the part that lies outside the operating workflow.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.h: F04.8 Decision-making in a machine bureaucracy
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S8
- concept_id: u6-machine-bureaucracy

A machine bureaucracy combines decentralized decision-making with few hierarchical layers and a wide span of control.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: A machine bureaucracy has centralized decision-making and a highly elaborated administrative structure with many layers and a low span of control. Decentralization belongs to the professional bureaucracy and the adhocracy.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S9
- concept_id: u6-management-levels

Drawing up next week's shift roster of an engine-assembly line is a strategic decision that belongs to top management.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: A weekly shift roster is an operational decision of low management (first-line supervisors). Top management takes the strategic, general decisions that affect the firm as a whole.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x:
- id: F04-S10
- concept_id: u6-controlling

Controlling involves establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations and taking corrective action if required, which is why planning and controlling are inseparable.

chunks.t: Decisions, structures and control
chunks.x: These are the four activities of controlling in the course, and the standards it measures against come from planning, so the two functions cannot be separated.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: Bank F05 — Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, 0 blank, a short reason for every answer). The examples PDF has no Topic 7 statement; content from Topic 7, Slides 5 and 12-19.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S1
- concept_id: u7-organizational-creativity

The creativity of an organization depends not only on the creativity of its individuals but also on the social processes and contextual factors that shape the way those individuals interact.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: The course defines organizational creativity as a function of the creativity of the individuals and of the social processes and contextual factors that shape their interaction; it is not a simple sum, because structure, routines and incentives can thwart or amplify individual creativity.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: F05.2 A minor change called radical
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S2
- concept_id: u7-radical-vs-incremental

A new coating that slightly extends the life of an existing turbine blade, without changing the blade or the engine, is a radical innovation, because it improves an aerospace product.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: A relatively minor change to existing practices is an incremental innovation; a radical innovation is very new and different from prior solutions. Improving a product does not make an innovation radical: the size of the departure from prior solutions does.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S3
- concept_id: u7-competence-perspective

The same innovation can be competence-enhancing for one firm and competence-destroying for another firm of the same industry.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: Whether an innovation enhances or destroys competences depends on whose perspective is taken: it enhances the competences of a firm whose existing knowledge base it builds on, and destroys those of a firm whose competences it does not use or renders obsolete.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: F05.4 A new display in the same panel
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S4
- concept_id: u7-architectural-vs-component

Replacing the analogue altimeter of a light aircraft with a digital one that fits the same slot of the instrument panel, without changing how the other systems of the aircraft interact, is an architectural innovation.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: A change to one component that does not significantly affect the overall configuration of the system is a component (modular) innovation. An architectural innovation changes the overall design of the system or the way its components interact with each other, which this change does not do.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: F05.5 Where the S-curve is steepest
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S5
- concept_id: u7-s-curve-shape

On the S-curve of technology performance, performance improves fastest when the first units of effort are invested in a new technology, and then grows more and more slowly.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: Plotted against effort, performance improves slowly at first, then quickly, and finally flattens as it approaches the limit of the technology. The steepest part is in the middle of the curve, not at its beginning.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S6
- concept_id: u7-s-curve-limit

When a technology reaches the flat upper part of its S-curve, additional effort brings only small improvements in performance, because the technology is approaching its limit.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: The upper part of the S-curve flattens towards the dotted line of the limit of the technology drawn on the slide, so each additional unit of effort yields a smaller gain in performance.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S7
- concept_id: u7-discontinuous-technology

A discontinuous technology fulfils a similar market need to the existing technology by building on an entirely new knowledge base, and at first its performance may be lower than that of the technology it later overtakes.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: This is the course's definition of a discontinuous technology; the second S-curve of the slide may start below the first technology and later cross it and reach a higher performance.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: F05.8 What the diffusion curve plots
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S8
- concept_id: u7-diffusion-vs-performance-curve

The S-curve of technology diffusion plots the performance of a technology against the effort invested in developing it.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: Performance against effort is the S-curve of technology performance. The diffusion S-curve plots the cumulative share of adopters against time (2.5%, 16%, 50%, 84% and 100% at the boundaries of the adopter categories), because diffusion is the spread of a technology through a population.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S9
- concept_id: u7-adopter-categories

The early majority and the late majority each account for about 34% of the adopters of a technology, so together they make up about two thirds of the market.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: The bell-shaped curve of market share gives 34% to the early majority and 34% to the late majority, 68% in total; innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%) and laggards (16%) make up the rest.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.h: F05.10 How a design becomes dominant
chunks.x:
- id: F05-S10
- concept_id: u7-dominant-design-selection

A design becomes dominant only when a regulator or standards body officially enforces it; learning effects and network externalities play no part in its selection.

chunks.t: Innovation types, S-curves and the dominant design
chunks.x: A dominant design is a de facto standard: it dominates its product category (usually 50% or more of the market) even if it is not officially enforced. The course gives learning effects and network externalities (installed base and complementary goods) as the reasons why dominant designs are selected.

chunks.t: Cash-flow profiles, timing of flows and payback
chunks.h: Bank F06 — Cash-flow profiles, timing of flows and payback
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten True/False statements written for the bank in the style of Exercise 4 of the examples PDF (+0.15 right, −0.15 wrong, 0 blank; the reasoning is required). Sources: 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf and 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercises 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9; Examples PDF, Exercises 5 and 6. The Topic 3 deck has no investment-selection slides, so the criteria are those used in the problem sheet and its key.

chunks.t: Cash-flow profiles, timing of flows and payback
chunks.h: F06.1 A negative flow after the outlay
chunks.x:
- id: F06-S1
- concept_id: u3-payback-negative-flow

The payback criterion cannot be applied to a project whose net cash flow in year 1 is negative.

chunks.t: Cash-flow profiles, timing of flows and payback
